CrewDeck is a desktop application that enables teams to manage and dispatch work to AI agents. Think of it as a project management tool (like Jira or Trello) specifically designed for AI-powered development workflows. With CrewDeck, you can: Organize work by team using Projects Connect GitHub repositories to discover AI agents and commands Create tasks on a visual Kanban board Execute tasks with AI agents that write code, create branches, and open Pull Requests Monitor progress in real-time through an integrated terminal

Concept Description Project A logical grouping for your work — typically representing a team, project, or domain (e.g., "Engineering", "Frontend", "API Team"). Repository A GitHub repo connected to a project. Agents and commands are automatically discovered from connected repos. Agent An AI specialist that can execute tasks. Examples include "frontend-developer", "code-reviewer", and "database-designer". Command A slash command (e.g., /build-feature, /fix-bug) that defines a specific workflow an agent can run. Task A work item on the Kanban board. Tasks have a title, description, priority, and can be assigned to agents. Task Number A human-readable identifier automatically assigned to each task (e.g., "ENG-0001"). Worktree A separate working directory for each task. This isolates changes and prevents conflicts with your local development. Config Claude Code configurations including agents, skills, and commands, managed from the Agents, Commands and Skills tabs under Crew in the project header. Skill A reusable workflow or specialized task automation that extends Claude's capabilities (e.g., /commit, /review-pr). Template Pre-built configurations that can be imported into a repository to quickly set up agents, skills, or commands.

Before using CrewDeck, ensure you have: Node.js 18+ — Download from nodejs.org Git — Version control system GitHub Account — For repository integration GitHub Personal Access Token — With repo scope enabled Claude Code CLI — The AI agent runtime
Download the CrewDeck installer for your platform Run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions Launch the CrewDeck application

Step 1: Connect GitHub​ CrewDeck supports two methods for authenticating with GitHub: Option A: Device Flow (Recommended — new in v0.15.0) GitHub authentication now supports OAuth Device Flow (RFC 8628), which eliminates port conflicts and does not require a locally running redirect server. Click Settings in the sidebar (gear icon at the bottom) In the GitHub Integration section, click Sign in with GitHub CrewDeck displays a short user code (e.g., ABCD-1234) Visit github.com/login/device in your browser Enter the code and authorize CrewDeck The app detects authorization automatically and shows a green "Connected" status indicator Option B: Personal Access Token (PAT) Click Settings in the sidebar (gear icon at the bottom) In the GitHub Integration section, click the token input field Go to github.com/settings/tokens and create a Personal Access Token: Click Generate new token (classic) Give it a descriptive name (e.g., "CrewDeck App") Select the repo scope (full control of private repositories) Click Generate token and copy the token Paste the token into CrewDeck and click Connect GitHub You should see a green "Connected" status indicator Step 2: Install Claude Code CLI​ The Claude Code CLI is required to execute tasks with AI agents. In the Settings page, you'll see instructions to install it: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code After installation, verify it works by running claude --version in your terminal. Step 3: Create Your First Project​ Click the + button next to "Projects" in the sidebar Enter a name (e.g., "Engineering" or "My Project") Optionally add a description and choose a color Click Create Project

Projects are the top-level organizational units. Each project has its own: Kanban board with tasks Connected GitHub repositories Discovered agents and commands Creating a Project​ In the sidebar, click the + button next to "Projects" Fill in the project details: Name (required): A short identifier (e.g., "Backend", "Mobile") Description (optional): A brief explanation of the project's purpose Color: Choose from 8 preset colors to help visually distinguish projects Click Create Project Navigating Projects​ Click any project in the sidebar to open it The Dashboard (home icon) shows all projects with their task counts and progress Each project card on the Dashboard displays: Project name and description Total task count Progress bar showing completion percentage Editing or Deleting a Project​ Currently, projects can be edited or deleted through the project settings. Be cautious when deleting — this removes all associated tasks. Per-Project Kanban Stage Selection​ Each project can be configured to show only the Kanban columns relevant to its workflow. The two required columns — To Do and Done — are always shown. The three optional columns can be toggled on or off per project. Optional Stages Stage Default When to Disable In Progress On Simple projects where tasks go directly from To Do to Done In Review On Projects without a formal code review step Document On Projects that don't produce documentation artifacts Configuring Stages When Creating a Project Click the + button next to "Projects" in the sidebar In the Kanban Stages section of the Create Project modal, uncheck any optional stages you don't need Click Create Project Configuring Stages for an Existing Project Open the project and click the project menu (three dots) Select Edit Project In the Kanban Stages section, toggle optional stages on or off Click Save Display Behavior for Tasks in Disabled Stages When a stage is disabled, tasks whose database status corresponds to that stage are displayed in the nearest preceding enabled stage. This is a display-only change — the task's actual status in the database is not modified. Re-enabling a stage causes tasks to reappear in their correct columns automatically. Assigning Claude Accounts to a Project​ Each project can be configured to draw Claude credits from one or more specific stored accounts, so parallel work across projects does not drain a single credit pool — and so that several sessions started at once in the same project do not all queue behind one account's rate limit. Configuring the Accounts for an Existing Project Open the project and click the project menu (three dots) Select Edit Project In the Claude Account section, tick each account this project should use Click Save Behavior No accounts ticked — Follows the account selected in Settings → Claude One account ticked — That account is used for every AI run started from the project, exactly as before Several accounts ticked — Each new agent session is handed the least-busy assigned account, so concurrent work spreads across them instead of stacking on one OAuth-only — The account picker appears only when Claude is authenticated with OAuth Fallback on removal — If an assigned account is later removed, the sessions that would have used it fall back to the default account, and the page shows a warning with a one-click button to drop the stale entries When an assigned account hits a rate limit, CrewDeck stops sending new sessions to it for a few minutes and may temporarily retry that project's runs with another stored account so work keeps moving. If every assigned account is busy, runs still start — they queue on the least-loaded one rather than failing. The app-wide default account is never changed by any of this. You can cap how many sessions run on a single account at once, and watch each account's current load, in Settings → Claude. Account assignment applies to agent sessions that CrewDeck runs for you. Terminal sessions you drive yourself use whatever account the Claude command-line tool is already signed in to. To add accounts, go to Settings → Claude.

To use AI agents, you need to connect at least one GitHub repository that contains agent definitions. Prerequisites​ GitHub must be connected in Settings (see First-Time Setup) You need access to at least one GitHub repository Connecting a Repository​ Navigate to your project Click the Repos tab Browse the list of available repositories from your GitHub account Click Connect next to the repository you want to add Wait for the repository to be cloned locally (this may take a moment for large repos) Once connected, CrewDeck automatically scans for agents and commands What Gets Discovered​ CrewDeck scans connected repositories for: Directory Content Result .claude/agents/ Agent definition files Available agents appear in the Agents tab .claude/commands/ Command definition files Available commands appear in the Commands tab Syncing Agents and Commands​ If you update agents or commands in your repository, use the Refresh button to pull changes and re-discover configurations: Go to the Repos tab in CrewDeck Click the Refresh button (circular arrow icon) next to the repository CrewDeck will: Pull the latest changes from the remote repository Re-scan for agents and commands Update the agent/command lists automatically Refresh Button Behavior Repository Type Action Primary/Context Repos Pulls latest, re-discovers agents and commands Marketplace Repos Pulls latest, re-discovers marketplace agents Error Handling The refresh operation may fail in certain situations: Error Cause Solution Uncommitted changes Repository has modified files Commit or stash changes before refreshing Network error No internet connection Check your connection and retry An error banner displays with specific instructions when refresh fails. Click the X to dismiss it. Disconnecting a Repository​ Go to the Repos tab Click Disconnect next to the repository you want to remove Creating a New Repository​ Instead of creating a repository on GitHub first and then connecting it, you can create a new GitHub repository directly from CrewDeck. How to Create a New Repository Navigate to your project's Repos tab Click the Create New Repo button (next to the repository list header) Fill in the repository details: Field Required Description Repository Name Yes Letters, numbers, hyphens, underscores, and periods only. Cannot start with a period or end with .git. Max 100 characters. Description No A brief description of the repository Visibility Yes Private (default) or Public Initialize with README No Checked by default; creates an initial README file Click Create Repository CrewDeck will: Create the repository on GitHub Clone it locally Connect it to the project Run agent and command discovery Error Handling If the clone step fails after the GitHub repository has been created, CrewDeck automatically deletes the orphaned GitHub repository to prevent leftover resources. Error Cause Solution Repository name already exists A repo with the same name exists on your GitHub account Choose a different name Clone failed Network error or permissions issue The orphaned repo is cleaned up automatically; retry the operation Permission denied Token lacks sufficient permissions Ensure your token has the repo scope Primary and Context Repositories​ When a project has multiple connected repositories, CrewDeck distinguishes between them using primary and context designations. How It Works Designation Description Primary The main working repository where code changes happen. The first connected repo is automatically set as primary. Shown with a blue "Primary" badge. Context Additional repositories that provide supplementary documentation. Shown with a purple "Context" badge when multiple repos are connected. Context repos contribute documentation from their docs/ folders and PROJECTS.md files to enhance AI-generated agent and command suggestions in the Generate wizard on the Agents, Commands and Skills tabs. Changing the Primary Repository Navigate to the Repos tab Find the context repository you want to make primary Click the Set Primary button The previous primary becomes a context repository Context caches are automatically refreshed Context in Config Generation When using the Generate wizard on the Agents, Commands or Skills tab: CrewDeck automatically fetches documentation from context repos A purple indicator shows "Context available from N connected repos" This context is included in the AI generation prompt for more relevant suggestions Alternative Branching Strategies​ By default, CrewDeck creates feature branches from the repository's default branch (usually main). Starting in v0.12.0, you can configure per-project branching strategies to match your team's workflow. Supported Strategies Strategy Description Branch Pattern Default Feature branches from the default branch feature/{task-slug}-{id} Trunk-Based Short-lived branches from main or trunk feature/{task-slug}-{id} GitFlow Feature branches from develop, releases from release/ feature/{task-slug}-{id} from develop Custom User-defined base branch per project Configurable Configuring a Branching Strategy Navigate to your project's Settings or Repos tab Select the branching strategy for the project For custom strategies, specify the base branch name All new task executions will use the configured strategy How It Works When a task starts execution, the worktree is created from the configured base branch instead of the default branch PR targets are automatically set to the correct base branch Existing tasks with worktrees are not affected by strategy changes

Tasks are the work items that AI agents will implement. They live on a Kanban board with five columns. Understanding the Kanban Board​ Column Status Description To Do todo Tasks waiting to be started In Progress in_progress Tasks currently being executed by an agent In Review in_review Tasks with completed code, awaiting review Document document Tasks with merged PRs, awaiting documentation Done done Completed tasks Creating a Task​ Navigate to your project's Board tab Click Add Task (or the + button) Fill in the task details: Field Required Description Title Yes A clear, descriptive name for the task Description No Detailed requirements, acceptance criteria, or context Priority Yes Low, Medium, or High (affects visual indicator) Agents No One or more agents to assign to this task Command No A specific command to run (e.g., /build-feature) Epic No Associate this task with a parent Epic Dependencies No Tasks this task depends on Click Create Task Two-Column Layout The Create Task modal uses a two-column grid layout on wider screens to reduce scrolling. Related shorter fields — such as Command and Agents, or Epic and Priority — appear side-by-side. Full-width fields like Title, Description, Attachments, and Dependencies span both columns. When Command mode is set to "chain", the Command and Agents sections expand to full width to accommodate the Command Chain Builder. Natural Language Task Creation​ CrewDeck can extract structured task details from natural language descriptions using AI, eliminating the need to manually fill in each form field. How to Use Click Add Task on the Kanban board Click the From Description tab in the Create Task modal Describe your task in natural language in the text area (up to 5,000 characters) Example: "We need to build a user authentication system with JWT tokens, password hashing using bcrypt, and email verification. This should work with our PostgreSQL database and include rate limiting for login attempts." Click Extract & Fill Form Wait for AI to analyze your description (~5-15 seconds) Review the auto-populated fields: Title: Concise imperative form (max 80 characters) Description: 2-3 sentence summary with acceptance criteria as a markdown checklist Priority: Assigned based on urgency and impact indicators Agents: Automatically matched to your project's available agents Confidence Score: Shows AI's confidence in the extraction quality Edit any fields as needed Click Create Task What Gets Extracted Field How It's Determined Title AI condenses description into an actionable task title Description AI rewrites as a clear summary with checklist acceptance criteria Priority Assigned based on keywords like "urgent", "critical", "nice-to-have" Suggested Agents Matched against your project's agents using name normalization Confidence 0-100% score indicating extraction quality Graceful Fallback If extraction fails (timeout, network error, or AI returns invalid JSON): Click Continue Manually to proceed with your original description pre-filled Your description is never lost — it's preserved in the form You can retry extraction or continue filling fields manually Tips for Best Results Include specific requirements, not just vague goals Mention technology stack or frameworks to help with agent matching Use urgency keywords for automatic priority assignment Keep descriptions focused on a single task (not multiple unrelated items) Auto-Task Decomposition​ Break down large epics or complex tasks into smaller, actionable subtasks automatically using AI. When to Use You have a large task that represents multiple smaller work items You want to parallelize work across multiple agents You need to establish dependencies between related subtasks You want AI to suggest optimal task sequencing How to Use Create or select a task in the "To Do" column that represents an epic Click on the task to open the detail view Click the Auto-decompose button Wait for AI analysis (~15-30 seconds) Review the suggested subtasks in the Decompose Task modal: Each subtask shows title, description, priority, suggested agents, commands, and dependencies Confidence scores indicate AI's certainty about each subtask Color-coded badges show confidence levels (green ≥70%, yellow ≥40%, red <40%) Select which subtasks to create (use Select All / Deselect All toggles) Edit any subtask details inline: Modify titles or descriptions by clicking on them Adjust priorities using the dropdown Click Create Selected Tasks Wait for subtask creation and dependency wiring Optionally rate the decomposition quality (1-5 stars) to improve future suggestions What AI Analyzes The decomposition service considers: The parent task title and description Your project's available agents and commands Historical patterns from similar tasks (via cross-task learning) Best practices for task sequencing and parallelization Automatic Dependency Wiring After creation: Inter-subtask dependencies: AI-suggested dependencies between subtasks (e.g., "Build API" must complete before "Build UI") Parent-child blocking: Each subtask automatically blocks the parent epic until all subtasks complete DAG validation: Circular dependencies are prevented Configuration Up to 20 subtasks can be generated per decomposition (configurable limit). The AI prefers fan-out/parallel patterns over linear chains to maximize parallelization opportunities. Quality Feedback Loop After creating subtasks, you can rate the decomposition quality: 1-5 star rating Optional comment for specific feedback Metrics tracked: subtasks generated, accepted, and modified This data improves future decomposition suggestions Epics​ Epics are high-level containers that group related tasks under a shared parent theme or source document. They provide a way to organize work that conceptually belongs together — such as all tasks derived from a product requirement document or a strategic initiative — without requiring each task to be a direct child in a strict hierarchy. Creating an Epic Navigate to your project's Board tab Click Add Task and fill in the task details as usual In the task creation form, enable the Epic toggle Provide a descriptive title that captures the parent theme (e.g., "Authentication Overhaul", "Q1 Performance Initiative") Click Create Task — the new task is marked as an epic with a distinct badge on the Kanban board Auto-Decomposing an Epic into Subtasks Epics can be automatically decomposed into a set of actionable subtasks using the same AI decomposition engine described in Auto-Task Decomposition: Open the epic task from the Kanban board Click Auto-decompose in the task detail view Review the AI-generated subtasks in the Decompose Task modal Select which subtasks to create and click Create Selected Tasks Each created subtask is automatically linked to the epic as a child Epic Badge and Progress Epic tasks display a dedicated badge on the Kanban card and in the task detail view: Element Description Epic badge Purple "Epic" label distinguishing it from standard tasks Child count Shows how many subtasks belong to this epic Progress bar Proportion of child tasks in "Done" status out of total children Linking Existing Tasks to an Epic You can associate existing tasks with an epic after creation: Open the task you want to link In the task detail view, find the Epic field Select the parent epic from the dropdown Click Save — the task now counts toward the epic's progress When to Use Epics Decomposing a large feature specification or product requirements document into parallel workstreams Grouping all tasks related to a single GitHub Issue or roadmap item Coordinating multi-team work where each subtask is owned by a different agent or developer Tracking high-level initiative progress on the Kanban board without losing granular task detail Epic Filter Pills — Conditional Visibility The Kanban board header displays epic filter pills so you can narrow the board to tasks belonging to a single epic. Filter pills only appear for epics that have at least one task currently visible on the board: Epics from past development cycles whose tasks are all released, failed, or deleted are automatically hidden from the filter bar If the currently selected epic filter becomes inactive (all its tasks disappear from the board), the filter resets to "All" automatically Epic badges on individual task cards continue to show the epic name regardless of filter visibility Task Numbers​ Each task automatically receives a unique task number based on the project name: Format: ABC-0001, ABC-0002, etc. The prefix is derived from the project name (e.g., "Engineering" → "ENG") Task numbers are sequential within each project Editing Tasks​ Click on a task card to open the detail view Modify the fields you want to change Click Save Note: Tasks can only be edited when in the "To Do" status. Once a task moves to "In Progress", it becomes read-only. Moving Tasks Between Columns​ Drag and drop: Click and hold the drag handle on a task card, then drag it to another column Tasks automatically update their status when moved to a new column Moving a task to "In Progress" does not automatically start execution — you need to click Run Deleting Tasks​ Click the Delete button (trash icon) on the task card Confirm the deletion when prompted Task Dependencies​ CrewDeck supports a comprehensive task dependency system that allows you to define prerequisite relationships between tasks, ensuring work happens in the correct order. Dependency Types Type Behavior Use Case Blocks Hard blocker — dependent task cannot start until this task completes Critical prerequisites (e.g., "API endpoints must be built before UI") Requires Informational — indicates the task needs output from another task but doesn't block execution Soft dependencies for awareness (e.g., "UI should use API patterns") Related Contextual relationship — shows tasks are related without blocking Grouping related work for visibility Adding Dependencies When creating a new task: In the Create Task modal, scroll to the Dependencies section Click Add Dependency Search for the task(s) this new task depends on Select the dependency type (Blocks, Requires, or Related) Add multiple dependencies as needed CrewDeck validates that no circular dependencies are created When editing an existing task (in "To Do" status): Open the task detail view Navigate to the Dependencies section Click Edit Dependencies Add or remove dependencies as needed Viewing Dependencies Task cards display a dependency badge showing: Amber badge: Task has unresolved blocking dependencies (cannot be started) Gray badge: All blocking dependencies are resolved (task is ready) Count: Number shown indicates total dependencies In the task detail view, you can see: Depends On: Tasks this task depends on (with status indicators) Required By: Tasks that depend on this task (reverse lookup) Dependency Enforcement The dependency system enforces constraints at multiple layers: UI: You cannot drag a task with unresolved blocking dependencies to "In Progress" Backend: API calls to start tasks with unresolved blocking dependencies are rejected Database: Circular dependencies are detected and prevented using DAG validation Circular Dependency Prevention CrewDeck automatically detects circular dependencies using a recursive database query: If adding a dependency would create a cycle (A depends on B, B depends on A), the operation is rejected This validation runs for all dependency types, not just "blocks" Maximum dependency chain depth is limited to 100 levels for safety Auto-Chaining for Generated Tasks When you use the Generate Tasks or Dispatch Tasks features: Tasks are automatically linked with sequential "blocks" dependencies Task 2 depends on Task 1, Task 3 depends on Task 2, etc. This creates an automatic execution pipeline for batch-generated work AI-Driven Dependency Suggestions CrewDeck can automatically suggest dependencies based on task content and project context. This feature uses AI to analyze task descriptions and recommend which tasks should depend on others, helping you build accurate dependency graphs without manual analysis. Example Workflows Frontend/Backend Split: Task A: "Build API endpoints" (no dependencies) Task B: "Build UI components" (blocks on Task A) Result: UI work cannot start until API is complete Parallel Work with Final Integration: Task A: "Design database schema" (no dependencies) Task B: "Build auth service" (blocks on Task A) Task C: "Build user service" (blocks on Task A) Task D: "Integration testing" (blocks on Task B and Task C) Result: Tasks B and C can run in parallel after A completes; D waits for both Task Templates​ Task templates allow you to create reusable task configurations with variable placeholders, streamlining repetitive task creation workflows. Creating a Task from Template Click New Task on the Kanban board Click the From Template button at the top of the modal Select a template from the list Fill in the variable values when prompted (e.g., {{feature_name}}, {{module_name}}) Review the interpolated task details Click Create Task Saving a Task as Template Open an existing task (click to view details) Click the Save as Template button Name your template Optionally add a category (backend, frontend, bugfix, etc.) Define variables by replacing specific values with {{variable_name}} placeholders Click Save Template Template Variables Variables use double curly braces: {{variable_name}} Example template title: Implement {{feature_name}} feature Example template description: Add {{feature_name}} to the {{module_name}} module. Acceptance Criteria: - {{acceptance_criteria}} Managing Templates Access template management from the Project page Crew → Templates tab: View all available templates grouped by category Edit existing templates Delete unused templates Import/export templates as JSON for sharing Browse 12 built-in starter templates covering common development tasks VCS-Driven Task Templates​ Task templates can be stored directly in your repository's version control system, enabling teams to share and evolve templates alongside their codebase. How It Works When VCS-driven templates are enabled, CrewDeck reads template definitions from a designated directory in the primary repository: .crewdeck/ templates/ backend-api-endpoint.yml frontend-component.yml bugfix-with-tests.yml Templates in this directory are automatically discovered when you open the "From Template" modal. They appear alongside locally stored templates with a git branch icon indicating their VCS origin. Template File Format VCS templates use YAML with the same field structure as locally created templates: name: "Backend API Endpoint" category: backend description: "Add a new REST endpoint with validation and tests" title: "Implement {{endpoint_name}} endpoint" body: | Add the `{{endpoint_name}}` endpoint to the `{{module_name}}` module. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] Route is registered in the router - [ ] Input validation with Zod schema - [ ] Unit tests cover happy path and error cases - [ ] {{additional_criteria}} variables: - name: endpoint_name description: "Name of the endpoint (e.g., create-user)" - name: module_name description: "Module the endpoint belongs to (e.g., auth, billing)" - name: additional_criteria description: "Any additional acceptance criteria" default: "OpenAPI spec is updated" Syncing Templates VCS templates are pulled from the repository each time you: Click Refresh on the repository in the Repos tab Open the "From Template" modal (templates are refreshed on open) Changes merged into the primary branch are reflected immediately after a repository sync. Team Sharing Workflow Create or edit a template file in .crewdeck/templates/ in your repository Commit and push the template file Open a PR for review — teammates can comment on the template before it is shared After the PR is merged, all team members see the new template on next sync Precedence When a locally stored template and a VCS template share the same name, the VCS template takes precedence. This ensures the canonical team version is always used. Automated Task Generation​ Let AI analyze your project roadmap and automatically generate actionable development tasks. How to Use Navigate to your project Ensure your repository has roadmap files in docs/roadmap/ directory Click the project menu button → Select Generate Tasks Click Generate Tasks in the modal Wait for AI to analyze your roadmap (~30-60 seconds) Review the 10 generated task suggestions with: Priority assignments (high, medium, low) Suggested agent assignments Suggested command mappings Click Create 10 Tasks to add all suggestions to the "To Do" column What Gets Analyzed The AI reads all .md files in your repository's docs/roadmap/ directory and extracts actionable work items, automatically assigning priorities and matching tasks to your project's agents and commands. Error Handling Error Solution No roadmap documents found Add .md files to docs/roadmap/ directory Claude CLI not available Install Claude CLI: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code Generation timeout Check network connection and retry Task Dispatcher​ Dispatch tasks from one project to another by analyzing documents like meeting notes or debate transcripts. Use Case When your CEO project holds a strategy debate and needs to delegate implementation tasks to your Engineering project, the Task Dispatcher automates this workflow. How to Use Navigate to the source project (e.g., CEO) Click the project menu button → Select Dispatch Tasks Select the target project from the dropdown Click Browse... to select a document file (debate transcript, meeting notes, etc.) Click Dispatch Tasks Wait for AI analysis (~30-60 seconds) Review the generated task suggestions Click Create X Tasks to add them to the target project What Gets Analyzed The AI analyzes any document you provide (Markdown, text, JSON) and generates tasks scoped to the target project's agents and commands. Key Features Cross-project task assignment AI-powered document analysis Automatic agent/command mapping to target project's resources Supports files up to 500KB Both established repos (creates PR) and new repos (direct commit) Importing GitHub Issues as Tasks​ Convert GitHub Issues from your connected repository directly into CrewDeck tasks. How to Use Navigate to your project Click the Actions dropdown menu in the project header Select Import Issues Select which GitHub Issues to import Issues are created as tasks in the "To Do" column with GitHub Issue metadata attached What Gets Imported Issue title becomes task title Issue description becomes task description Issue number is linked to the task Labels are preserved as task tags Note: As of v0.11.0, the Import Issues button has been relocated from the Board header to the Actions dropdown menu for better organization. Creating a GitHub Issue Without Leaving CrewDeck​ File a GitHub issue from inside the app. CrewDeck reads the target repository's own issue templates (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/) and renders them as a native form, so the issue you create carries the same headings, labels and title prefix as one filed through GitHub's website. Two Entry Points Sidebar → Issues — files against the public CrewDeck issue tracker. Use this to report a bug in CrewDeck itself or to request a feature. Project → Actions → Create Issue — files against the project's primary repository. The item is disabled with a "Connect a repository to this project" tooltip until the project has at least one connected repo. How to Use Open either entry point above Pick a template from the chooser. Repositories that publish no templates skip this step and open a plain title-and-description form Fill in the fields. Required fields are marked and checked before anything is sent Click Create issue The success view shows the new issue number, its title and the labels the template applied, with an Open on GitHub button Round-Tripping Into Tasks Creating an issue does not create a task. To bring it onto the board, use Actions → Import Issues as described above — the new issue appears in the list like any other. Contact Links If the repository's config.yml defines contact links (documentation, a security mailbox), the chooser lists them below the templates. They open in your default browser. A repository that disables blank issues offers no free-form option, matching what GitHub's own chooser does. If Something Goes Wrong Every failure state explains itself and offers Open on GitHub instead, which opens the normal browser issue form — so a signed-out session, an exhausted API rate limit or a dropped connection is never a dead end. Signing in to GitHub is done under Settings → Integrations. Importing JIRA Issues as Tasks​ Connect your Atlassian JIRA Cloud instance to import issues directly into CrewDeck as tasks. Setting Up JIRA Integration Navigate to Settings Scroll to the JIRA Integration section Enter your JIRA Cloud instance URL (e.g., https://yourteam.atlassian.net) Provide an API token generated from your Atlassian account's API token management page Enter your JIRA email address Click Connect to validate and save the credentials Importing Issues Navigate to your project Click the Actions dropdown menu in the project header Select Import JIRA Issues Select the JIRA project and filter by status or label Choose which issues to import Issues are created as tasks in the "To Do" column with JIRA metadata attached What Gets Imported JIRA Field CrewDeck Field Summary Task title Description Task description Priority Task priority (mapped: Highest/High to High, Medium to Medium, Low/Lowest to Low) Issue Key Linked as external reference Labels Preserved as task tags Bidirectional Sync When a CrewDeck task linked to a JIRA issue changes status, the corresponding JIRA issue is updated automatically: Task moved to "In Progress" transitions JIRA issue to your configured "In Progress" status Task moved to "Done" transitions JIRA issue to "Done" Sync is one-directional from CrewDeck to JIRA (JIRA changes do not flow back automatically) Requirements JIRA Cloud instance (Server/Data Center not supported) API token with read/write access to the target JIRA project Network access to *.atlassian.net from your machine Bidirectional GitHub Issue Sync​ CrewDeck maintains a live two-way link between tasks and GitHub Issues. Changes flow in both directions automatically, so your Kanban board and GitHub Issues stay in sync without manual effort. Pushing a Task to GitHub as an Issue Open a task in the detail view Click Push to GitHub Issue in the task header CrewDeck creates a GitHub Issue in the project's primary repository using the task title, description, priority, and status A purple GitHub Issue badge appears on the task card and links directly to the issue Importing GitHub Issues as Tasks Click Import Issues from the Board header or the project Actions menu Select one or more open issues from the list Click Import Selected Issues are created as tasks in the "To Do" column, linked to their source issue Automatic Status Sync Once a task is linked to a GitHub Issue, CrewDeck polls for changes every 60 seconds: When the task moves to "Done", the GitHub Issue is automatically closed When the GitHub Issue is closed externally, the task status updates to match Conflict resolution uses "last write wins" — whichever side was updated most recently takes precedence Label Mapping CrewDeck uses crewdeck: prefixed labels to map task metadata to GitHub Issues: CrewDeck Status GitHub Label To Do crewdeck:todo In Progress crewdeck:in-progress In Review crewdeck:in-review Document crewdeck:documenting Done crewdeck:done Priority labels (crewdeck:priority-low, crewdeck:priority-medium, crewdeck:priority-high) and a task-specific label (crewdeck:task-{taskNumber}) are also applied for full traceability. Requirements GitHub must be connected in Settings with a token that has the repo scope The project must have a primary repository configured Suggested Next Tasks​ AI-powered task suggestions appear automatically on your project dashboard, providing intelligent recommendations based on your project's context. Location A collapsible panel displays at the top of the Kanban board tab when active suggestions are available. The panel automatically hides when no suggestions exist. Suggestion Details Each suggestion card shows: Task title and description Confidence percentage (color-coded: green ≥80%, yellow ≥50%, gray <50%) Priority badge Suggested agents and commands Expandable rationale explaining why this task is recommended Matched criteria badges Actions Action Description Create Task Creates a new task from the suggestion in the "To Do" column Dismiss Removes the suggestion from the active list Creating Tasks from Suggestions Review the suggestion details Click Create Task on the card The system automatically: Creates the task with the suggested title and description Assigns suggested agents Maps suggested commands Marks the suggestion as accepted Intelligent Agent Selection​ When creating or editing tasks, CrewDeck provides AI-powered agent recommendations based on semantic similarity, historical performance, and user preferences. How It Works The recommendation system uses a hybrid scoring algorithm: Component Weight Description Composite Ranking 60% Agent's overall ranking (success rate, efficiency, satisfaction, recency) Semantic Similarity 40% Embedding-based match between task and successful historical tasks User Override Boost +0-15% Time-decayed boost when you've manually selected this agent for similar tasks Viewing Recommendations When you create a task, the system automatically shows the top 3 recommended agents with: Confidence percentage: Blend of ranking confidence and data confidence Composite ranking score: Agent's overall ranking out of 100 Similarity indicator: "AI-powered recommendations" when using embeddings User-preferred badge: Green indicator when you've frequently chosen this agent Score breakdown: Click to see detailed ranking components Agent Recommendation Details Each recommendation card displays: Field Description Confidence Overall confidence percentage (color-coded: green ≥80%, blue ≥60%, yellow ≥40%, gray <40%) Ranking Composite ranking score showing agent's overall performance Similarity Semantic similarity to successful historical tasks (when embeddings are available) Rationale Explanation of why this agent is recommended How to Use Create a new task or edit an existing one Review the recommended agents section Click on a recommended agent to assign it to the task Alternatively, browse all available agents and select manually When you override recommendations, the system learns your preferences for future suggestions Override Feedback Loop When you select a different agent than recommended: The system records your choice as an override Future recommendations for similar tasks receive a confidence boost for your chosen agent Override boosts decay over 30 days with exponential fallback Maximum boost is capped at 15% to prevent over-fitting to recent choices Similarity Methods The system uses a 3-tier fallback for similarity scoring: Embedding similarity (primary): Uses local Ollama (nomic-embed-text) embeddings to compare task semantics TF-based keyword similarity (fallback): Term-frequency cosine similarity when Ollama is unavailable Ranking-only (fallback): Pure ranking scores when no similarity method is available Configuration Navigate to Settings > Task Intelligence to: View recommendation statistics Clear override history Verify Ollama connectivity status File Attachments​ Attach files to tasks to provide additional context for AI agents during execution. Attaching a File Open a task in the detail view Click the Attach File button Select a file from your filesystem The file is stored locally and linked to the task How Attachments Are Used Attached files are automatically available to AI agents during task execution Files are stored in CrewDeck's local data directory for retrieval Attachments persist with the task throughout its lifecycle Marking Tasks as Failed​ When a task fails during execution or produces unsatisfactory results, you can explicitly mark it as failed to track failures in analytics and optionally recreate the task for retry. How to Mark a Task as Failed Locate the task on the Kanban board Click the warning icon on the task card, or open the task detail view and click Mark as Failed A confirmation dialog appears Optionally check Recreate this task with the same configuration to create a copy in the "To Do" column Click Confirm What Happens When a Task Is Marked as Failed Action Description Failure recorded A failure outcome is recorded in the outcome tracking system for analytics Task hidden The task is moved to "Done" status and hidden from the Kanban board Task recreated (optional) A new task with identical configuration (title, description, agents, commands, priority) appears in the "To Do" column Recreated Task Configuration When you check the recreate option, the new task copies: Title and description Priority level Assigned agents and commands Command chain configuration (if any) AI tool and model selection Agent execution mode The recreated task starts fresh in the "To Do" status. Failure Pattern Detection​ When tasks fail or partially complete, CrewDeck automatically analyzes terminal output and execution data to detect failure patterns and suggest intelligent recovery strategies. How It Works When you open a failed or partially completed task, the Failure Suggestion Panel automatically: Analyzes terminal output for error patterns using regex detection Compares task duration against category averages to detect timeouts Searches historical recovery data for matching patterns Finds similar tasks that succeeded after facing the same issue Generates prioritized retry suggestions with confidence scores Detected Failure Patterns Pattern Type Detection Method Example Errors Timeout Regex + duration analysis ETIMEDOUT, deadline exceeded, duration >3x category average Missing Dependency Regex module not found, ENOENT, command not found Agent Mismatch Regex agent not found, unsupported tool, capability not available Resource Exhaustion Regex ENOMEM, heap out of memory, disk full, rate limit Permission Error Regex EACCES, EPERM, 403 Forbidden, 401 Unauthorized Retry Strategies Each detected pattern maps to specific recovery strategies: Pattern Strategy Recommended Action Timeout Increase Timeout Increase execution timeout or break task into smaller steps Missing Dependency Install Dependency Install missing dependencies or verify environment setup Agent Mismatch Reassign Agent Choose a more suitable agent for this task type Resource Exhaustion Reduce Scope Reduce task scope or increase resource limits Permission Error Fix Permissions Fix file or API permissions before retrying Using the Failure Suggestion Panel The panel appears automatically in the task detail view when a task has failed or partially completed: Detected Patterns Section: Shows all identified failure patterns with confidence badges Color-coded confidence: green ≥80%, yellow ≥50%, gray <50% Evidence snippets from terminal output Recovery Suggestions Section: Displays prioritized recovery strategies Strategy name and description Confidence percentage Parameter changes to apply (if any) Apply button to record that you're trying this strategy Confirm Recovery button (after retry) to confirm the strategy worked Recovery History Section: Lists previously applied recoveries for this task Shows which strategies were attempted Confirmation status Timestamp Confidence Scoring Confidence Source Base Score Boost Pattern match 60% - Historical confirmed recovery 60% +15% Similar task recovery 30% - Duration-based timeout 60% - Suggestions below 10% confidence are filtered out automatically. Recovery Feedback Loop Improve future suggestions by recording recovery results: Open a failed task Review suggested recovery strategies Click Apply on a suggestion you want to try Retry the task with the suggested changes If the retry succeeds, return to the original failed task Click Confirm Recovery to mark the strategy as successful Confirmed recoveries boost confidence for matching patterns in future failures (project-scoped) Security & Safety Terminal output pre-truncated to 10KB before regex matching to prevent ReDoS attacks Evidence strings capped at 500 chars, max 5 items per pattern All regex patterns configurable in backend constants Task Intelligence and Semantic Search​ CrewDeck includes an AI-powered task intelligence system that generates semantic embeddings for tasks and enables similarity-based search to find related work. What are Task Embeddings? Task embeddings are 768-dimensional vector representations of your task titles and descriptions. They capture the semantic meaning of tasks, allowing the system to find conceptually similar tasks even when they use different wording. Generating Embeddings Task embeddings are generated automatically in the background using a local Ollama model (nomic-embed-text). No external API keys are required — the system runs entirely on your local machine. Ensure Ollama is running locally with the nomic-embed-text model pulled Embeddings are generated automatically when tasks are created or updated Embeddings are cached locally in SQLite Finding Similar Tasks Use semantic search to find tasks related to your current work: Open any task detail view Click Find Similar Tasks The system searches for tasks in the same project with high similarity scores Results show similarity percentages and highlight conceptually related work Similarity Scoring Cosine similarity algorithm compares embedding vectors Minimum similarity threshold: 30% Only compares tasks within the same project Results ranked by relevance (highest similarity first) Keyword Fallback If Ollama is unavailable, the system automatically falls back to TF-based (term frequency) keyword matching: Tokenizes task text and removes stop words Computes term frequencies Maps to a 100-dimensional keyword vector Provides basic similarity search without local model dependency Circuit Breaker Protection The system includes a circuit breaker to prevent cascading failures: Closed: Normal Ollama operation Open: After 3 consecutive failures, switches to keyword fallback for 60 seconds Half-Open: After cooldown, tries one Ollama call. Success closes circuit; failure reopens it Use Cases Find previous tasks that solved similar problems Identify duplicate or overlapping work Discover related tasks for dependency planning Build context when starting new tasks Privacy & Security Embeddings generated locally via Ollama — no data sent to external APIs Embeddings cached locally in SQLite Expired embeddings automatically cleaned up after TTL

The power of CrewDeck lies in its ability to have AI agents implement your tasks automatically. Prerequisites for Execution​ Before running a task, ensure: ✅ At least one repository is connected to the project ✅ At least one agent is discovered from a connected repo ✅ Claude Code CLI is installed (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code) ✅ The task has a title (description is optional but helpful) Running a Task​ Locate the task on the Kanban board (in the "To Do" column) Click the Run button on the task card The task moves to "In Progress" and the terminal panel opens What Happens During Execution​ When you click Run, the following phases execute automatically: Phase What Happens 1. Worktree Creation A separate Git worktree is created for the task, isolating it from your main codebase 2. Branch Creation A feature branch is created (e.g., feature/add-login-form-abc123) 3. Prompt Refinement The task description is enriched with project context 4. Prompt Saved The refined prompt is saved to prompts/build/ in the worktree 5. Initial Commit The prompt file is committed to the branch 6. Push to Remote The branch is pushed to GitHub 7. Draft PR Created A draft Pull Request is opened on GitHub 8. Command Execution The selected command runs (e.g., /build-feature) 9. Code Committed Any generated code is committed and pushed 10. PR Ready The PR is marked as "Ready for Review" Monitoring Progress​ The Terminal Panel shows real-time output from the AI agent Phase changes are logged so you can track progress The task card shows the current branch name and worktree path Interacting During Execution​ The terminal is fully interactive: You can type input if the AI agent asks questions Press Enter to submit your response The agent can prompt you for clarification or decisions When Execution Completes​ On success: The task moves to "In Review" status A PR link appears on the task card Click the PR link to view the Pull Request on GitHub On failure: The terminal shows error output The draft PR is preserved so you can manually complete the task Check the terminal output for troubleshooting information Command Chaining​ Execute multiple commands sequentially in a single task for complex multi-step workflows. Creating a Command Chain When creating or editing a task, navigate to the Command section Click the Chain toggle (switches from Single to Chain mode) Click Add Command to add commands to your chain Commands execute in the order they appear Use the up/down buttons to reorder steps Click the X button to remove a step Chain Settings When you have 2 or more steps, the Chain Settings section appears: Continue on Error: Toggle on to continue executing remaining steps even if one fails Off (default): Stops execution at the first failed step On: Marks failed steps but continues with remaining steps Execution Behavior When a task with a command chain runs: Each step displays with an ASCII art header showing step number Steps execute sequentially in order Status indicators update in real-time: Pending: Gray dot Running: Blue pulsing dot Completed: Green dot Failed: Red dot Skipped: Yellow dot (when continuing after error) Task card shows compact progress view (e.g., "2/5 steps (1 failed)") Summary displays total steps and any failures after completion Use Cases Common command chain workflows: Lint → Test → Build → Deploy Code Review → Fix Issues → Re-test Generate → Review → Document Sequential, Swarm, and Team Execution Modes​ When assigning two or more agents to a task, you can choose how those agents execute by selecting an Agent Execution Mode. The mode toggle appears automatically when 2+ agents are assigned. Choosing an Execution Mode When creating or editing a task, assign 2 or more agents The Agent Execution Mode toggle appears below the agent list Click Sequential, Swarm, or Team to select your mode Execution Modes Mode Description Best For Sequential (default) Agents execute one after another in the order listed. Each agent must complete before the next starts. Predictable workflows where order matters (e.g., build then test) Swarm An orchestrator agent coordinates subagents dynamically using Claude's Task tool, enabling parallel work within a single session. Complex tasks where multiple specialists can work simultaneously but share context Team A lead agent spawns fully independent Claude Code teammate instances that communicate via shared task lists and messaging. Large-scale tasks requiring truly independent agents with separate context windows Sequential Mode Details Agents run in the exact order they appear in the agent list If an agent fails, execution stops and the remaining agents do not run Terminal output shows clear markers for each agent's execution: Agent: @agent-name In relay mode (v0.19.0), each agent can pass structured context to the next agent via handoff files, enabling explicit knowledge transfer between sequential steps. Swarm Mode Details An orchestrator agent is used to coordinate work across subagents using Claude's Task tool If the first selected agent is an orchestrator type (e.g., feature-orchestrator, bugfix-orchestrator), it is used as the coordinator If no orchestrator is selected, the first agent in the list becomes the coordinator Subagents run within the orchestrator's session and share the same context window Terminal output indicates swarm mode with: Swarm Execution (Orchestrated) Team Mode Details Uses Claude Code's experimental Agent Teams feature A lead agent (preferably an orchestrator) coordinates fully independent teammate instances The lead uses TeamCreate, TaskCreate, and SendMessage tools to spawn and manage teammates Each teammate is a fully independent Claude Code instance with its own context window Teammates self-coordinate via a shared task list and can communicate directly Best suited for very large tasks where each agent needs complete independence Terminal output indicates team mode with: Team Execution (Agent Teams) in amber Example Workflows Sequential: Assign frontend-developer and code-reviewer to a task. The frontend developer implements the feature first, then the code reviewer analyzes the output. Swarm: Assign feature-orchestrator, frontend-developer, and backend-developer. The orchestrator coordinates both developers using the Task tool to work on their respective portions. Team: Assign feature-orchestrator, frontend-developer, backend-developer, and database-designer for a large multi-component feature. The orchestrator spawns each as an independent teammate with full context isolation. Task Execution Customizations​ By default, every task runs through three automatic execution phases: prompt refinement before coding begins, code review after the PR is created, and code improvement following the review. These phases can be disabled per-project when they add overhead without value. Configurable Phases Phase Default Command Stage Purpose Prompt Refinement refine-prompt Before In Progress Enriches task description with project context Code Review review-pr In Review Automated review of the created PR Code Improvement improve-pr In Review Applies review feedback automatically Configuring Phases Open the Create Project or Edit Project modal Scroll to the Task Execution section For each phase, choose between: Default (command-name) — runs the standard command None (skip) — disables the phase entirely for this project Save the project Behavior When Phases Are Disabled Disabling prompt refinement skips the pre-step; the task description is used as-is Disabling both review and improvement phases also skips marking the PR as "Ready for Review" — the PR remains a draft until you manually mark it ready These settings apply only to new task executions; tasks already in progress are not affected Unconfigured projects use the default behavior (all phases enabled) Security Phase command values are validated against an allowlist on every read. Invalid or injected values are silently replaced with the default command, preventing command injection even if the settings database were compromised. Pause and Resume Task Execution​ CrewDeck allows you to pause long-running task executions and resume them later, preserving the Claude CLI conversation context. Pausing a Running Task Locate a task with an active running session (look for the session indicator on the task card) Click the amber Pause button (⏸) next to the session indicator A confirmation dialog appears asking you to confirm the pause — this prevents accidental interruption of long-running agent work (see Terminal Session Confirmation Dialogs) Confirm the pause to gracefully terminate the PTY process and save the execution state The task shows a "Paused" indicator with the pause timestamp What Gets Saved When you pause a task, CrewDeck saves: Claude CLI session ID for resume capability Current command chain position (if using command chaining) Execution phase at time of pause Assigned agent IDs Worktree path and branch name This state is persisted to a .crewdeck-pause-state.json file in the task's worktree. Resuming a Paused Task Locate the paused task (it will show an amber "Paused" badge) Click the Resume button (▶) CrewDeck spawns a new terminal session and attempts to resume using Claude CLI's --resume flag If a session ID is available, it runs: claude --resume "<session-id>" If no session ID is found, it uses: claude --continue to continue from the last checkpoint Resume Behavior The resumed session picks up where the paused session left off Claude maintains conversation context across the pause/resume cycle Terminal output continues in a new session If resume fails, the pause state is restored so you can try again Use Cases Resource management: Pause tasks to free up terminal sessions for higher-priority work Work breaks: Pause long-running tasks during breaks without losing context Session limits: Manage concurrent session limits by pausing lower-priority tasks Context preservation: Keep Claude's conversation state across application restarts Session Resume​ In addition to pausing and resuming the current task, CrewDeck supports resuming a specific previous Claude CLI session by ID. This is useful when you want to return to an earlier session that was not paused through the standard flow. Using Session Resume Open the terminal panel for a task that has an existing worktree Click the Resume Session button in the terminal toolbar A session picker dialog appears listing recent Claude CLI sessions associated with this task Select the session you want to resume CrewDeck spawns a new PTY with claude --resume "<session-id>" Claude restores the conversation context from the selected session When to Use Session Resume Application restart: Resume a session that was running before CrewDeck was restarted Crash recovery: Pick up a session that was interrupted by a crash or system sleep Exploratory work: Return to a previous session to try a different approach Limitations Session resume requires the original worktree to still exist If Claude CLI cannot find the session (e.g., it was garbage-collected), an error is displayed in the terminal Only sessions from the current task's worktree are shown in the picker Command Approval Workflow​ CrewDeck includes a user-controlled command approval UI that lets you review commands before they execute in a terminal session. This is particularly useful for commands classified as "elevated" or when you want explicit oversight of what agents run on your behalf. How It Works When a command is classified as requiring approval, the terminal session pauses at the approval gate and displays the command details: The terminal panel shows an Approval Required banner at the top of the active session tab The banner displays: The full command string to be executed The working directory (worktree path) The risk classification label (Elevated or Dangerous) A brief explanation of why approval is requested You can Approve or Reject the command: Approve: The command proceeds immediately Reject: The command is blocked; the agent receives a rejection message and may prompt for an alternative approach Approval Timeout If you do not respond within 5 minutes, the approval request automatically times out and the command is rejected. The timeout countdown is displayed in the approval banner. Configuring Approval Behavior Navigate to Settings > Terminal > Command Approval to: Setting Description Require approval for elevated commands Toggle on (default) to gate commands classified as elevated risk Require approval for dangerous commands Toggle on (default) to gate commands classified as dangerous Auto-approve safe commands Always on; safe commands never require approval Approval timeout Duration before an unanswered request is auto-rejected (default: 5 minutes) Audit Log All approval decisions are recorded in the event sourcing store with: Command string (truncated to 500 characters) Decision (approved/rejected/timed out) Timestamp Session ID and task ID You can review approval history via the Security Dashboard.

The Terminal Panel displays real-time output from task executions and other terminal operations. Opening the Terminal​ The terminal opens automatically when you: Click Run on a task Open a terminal session manually Terminal Controls​ Control Action Minimize Collapses the terminal to a small bar at the bottom Maximize Expands the terminal to full screen Restore Returns to the default side panel view Close/X Terminates the session and closes the panel Multiple Sessions​ CrewDeck supports up to 20 concurrent terminal sessions, allowing you to run multiple AI agents in parallel. When multiple tasks are running: Each task gets its own terminal session Use the tabs at the top of the terminal to switch between sessions The active session is highlighted Each tab shows the task name or session identifier Session Scaling The terminal system automatically manages resources as you run more sessions: Sessions Scrollback Buffer Output Buffer 1-5 1000 lines 200KB 6-10 500 lines 120KB 11-15 250 lines 80KB 16-20 100 lines 60KB You can configure the maximum concurrent sessions in Terminal Settings (default: 10, max: 20). Advanced Features Adaptive Output Batching: System automatically adjusts batching intervals (20-50ms) based on output volume for optimal performance Error Recovery: Automatic crash recovery preserves output and allows session reconnection Memory Management: Dynamic buffer sizing prevents memory issues during heavy terminal usage Multi-Session Performance (new in v0.15.0) When running 5 or more concurrent sessions, CrewDeck automatically applies additional optimizations: Optimization Description WebGL Renderer Automatically promoted at 5+ sessions for GPU-accelerated rendering, reducing CPU load Graduated Flow Control Output backpressure is applied progressively to prevent oscillation during heavy output bursts Visibility-Gated Writes Background (non-visible) sessions defer rendering writes, reducing CPU usage for hidden sessions by approximately 60% Dynamic PTY Pool Sizing Idle PTY processes are pooled and resized dynamically, saving 10-30MB per idle process Faster Memory Compaction Idle sessions compact memory after 5 seconds (previously 30 seconds), reducing renderer memory usage by approximately 40% Project-Scoped Sessions​ Terminal sessions are automatically filtered based on which project you're viewing: Dashboard view: Shows all terminal sessions across all projects Project view: Shows only sessions for tasks in that project This helps reduce clutter when working with multiple projects. Sessions continue running in the background when you switch projects — they are not terminated. Activity Indicators When a project has running terminal sessions, its entry in the sidebar displays a subtle pulsing glow effect, making it easy to see which projects have active work. Session Reconnection​ Terminal sessions persist across page refreshes: If you refresh the browser window, sessions automatically reconnect Recent output (up to 50KB) is restored Running processes continue uninterrupted This prevents Claude API token waste from creating duplicate sessions Note: Session reconnection happens automatically when the app loads. You don't need to take any action. Session Status​ Status Indicator Running Animated spinner or activity indicator Completed Check mark or static icon Failed Error indicator Terminating a Process​ If a task is stuck or you need to stop execution: Click the X or Terminate button on the terminal tab Confirm the termination The process will be killed, but any committed work is preserved Opening a Standalone Terminal​ You can open an interactive terminal in a task's worktree directory: Find the task card with a worktree path Click the Open Terminal button A new terminal session opens in that directory New in v0.11.0: Interactive terminal sessions now open directly in the task's worktree directory instead of your HOME directory, making it easier to run commands in the correct project context without manual navigation. Pause and Resume Output​ During long-running terminal sessions with high-volume output, you can manually pause the terminal output to read specific content or reduce visual noise. While paused, output continues to be buffered in the background. How to Pause Output Locate the running terminal session Click the Pause button (two vertical bars icon) on the terminal tab The button turns yellow and switches to a Play icon A status bar indicator shows "Paused: X.XKB buffered" How to Resume Output Click the Play button (triangle icon) on the terminal tab All buffered output flushes to the terminal immediately Normal output streaming resumes Buffer Management Feature Details Buffer limit 500KB per session Warning threshold At 80% capacity (400KB), the indicator turns orange with a warning message Overflow behavior When the buffer is full, oldest data is dropped (FIFO) to preserve the most recent output Session independence Each terminal session has its own pause state; pausing one does not affect others Visual States State Indicator Not paused Gray pause icon Paused Yellow play icon + "Paused: X.XKB buffered" in status bar Buffer warning Orange warning icon + "Buffer nearly full: X.XKB buffered" Note: The underlying process continues running while output is paused. Only the rendering to the terminal UI is halted. This is different from the automatic throttle feature, which activates when output rate exceeds system limits. If both throttle and pause are active, only the pause indicator is shown. Terminal Keyboard Shortcuts​ CrewDeck includes a keyboard shortcut manager for the terminal panel. Shortcuts are scoped to terminal context so they do not conflict with system-wide or application-wide bindings. Default Shortcuts Shortcut Scope Action Ctrl+C Terminal focused Send interrupt signal (SIGINT) to active process Ctrl+D Terminal focused Send EOF to active process Ctrl+L Terminal focused Clear visible terminal screen (does not discard scroll history) Ctrl+Shift+C Terminal focused Copy selected text to clipboard Ctrl+Shift+V Terminal focused Paste from clipboard Ctrl+Shift+Up Terminal panel Scroll up one line in terminal history Ctrl+Shift+Down Terminal panel Scroll down one line in terminal history Ctrl+Shift+Home Terminal panel Jump to the beginning of terminal scroll history Ctrl+Shift+End Terminal panel Jump to the bottom (most recent output) Ctrl+Tab Terminal panel Switch to next session tab Ctrl+Shift+Tab Terminal panel Switch to previous session tab Shortcut Scoping Terminal keyboard shortcuts only activate when the terminal panel has focus. When typing in a task form, search bar, or other input field, terminal shortcuts are inactive to prevent accidental actions. Customizing Shortcuts Navigate to Settings > Terminal > Keyboard Shortcuts to: View all registered shortcuts and their current bindings Reassign shortcuts to different key combinations Reset all shortcuts to their defaults Terminal Session Confirmation Dialogs​ To prevent accidental data loss, the terminal panel now shows confirmation dialogs before performing destructive session operations. When Dialogs Appear Action Dialog Trigger Dialog Text Pause session Clicking Pause (⏸) on a running session "Pausing will suspend the active agent process. Any uncommitted work in the PTY session may be lost. Confirm pause?" Terminate session Clicking Terminate (✕) on a running session "Terminating will kill the active process immediately. This cannot be undone. Confirm termination?" Close terminal tab Clicking X on a running session tab Same as Terminate dialog Dialog Controls Each confirmation dialog provides: A clear description of the action and its consequences Cancel button (default focus) — dismisses the dialog and leaves the session unchanged Confirm button — proceeds with the destructive action The Cancel button receives keyboard focus by default so that pressing Enter or Space cancels the operation rather than confirming it, protecting against accidental confirmation from rapid key presses. Suppressing Dialogs If you frequently pause or terminate sessions and find the dialogs disruptive, you can suppress them: In the confirmation dialog, check Don't ask again for [action] Future clicks on Pause or Terminate execute immediately without a dialog To re-enable dialogs, navigate to Settings > Terminal and toggle Show confirmation dialogs Terminal Scroll History​ The terminal panel now maintains the complete scroll history for each session, allowing you to review all output from the beginning of a session — not just the most recently buffered lines. Scrolling to the Top Use any of the following methods to navigate terminal history: Press Ctrl+Shift+Home to jump to the beginning of the session history Click the Scroll to Top button (upward chevron icon) that appears in the terminal panel header when the scroll position is not at the bottom Use the scrollbar on the right side of the terminal to drag to any position History Limits Scroll history is subject to the same buffer limits as the session scrollback (see Session Scaling table). When the buffer is full, the oldest lines are discarded. The Scroll to Top button takes you to the oldest available line, which may not be the literal first line of the session for very high-output sessions. Scroll Position Indicator When you have scrolled up from the bottom, the terminal header displays: A "Scrolled" indicator showing you are viewing historical output A Jump to Bottom button (downward chevron) to return to live output instantly New output continues to be buffered and displayed at the bottom while you scroll through history. The terminal does not auto-scroll to the bottom while you are reading history unless you explicitly click Jump to Bottom. Save Terminal Output to File​ Export the complete output from any terminal session as a clean, human-readable log file. How to Save Output From the task detail view: Open the task by clicking on its card Click the Save Output (download icon) button in the modal header A native OS save dialog appears with a default filename based on the task number and date (e.g., ENG-0001_2026-02-25.log) Choose a destination and confirm From the terminal panel: In the terminal panel tab bar, locate a completed session tab Click the Save Output (download icon) button on the tab Choose a destination in the save dialog What Gets Saved ANSI escape codes are automatically stripped, producing a clean plain-text log file Color codes, cursor movement sequences, and terminal control characters are removed The resulting file is readable in any text editor or can be ingested by external log analysis tools Behavior Outcome Result Save successful Dialog closes silently User cancels No error shown; nothing is written No output available Error banner appears with a descriptive message Write failure Dismissible red error banner appears Output Priority The system retrieves output from three sources in priority order, maximizing the chance of recovering complete logs: In-memory circular buffer (most complete, up to 10 MB) Ring buffer from the virtualized terminal renderer Legacy database column (fallback for older sessions) Download Formatted Markdown Transcript​ In addition to saving raw terminal output, CrewDeck can generate a structured Markdown transcript of a task's terminal session. The transcript includes task metadata (task number, title, phase, status, duration, branch, PR link, and worktree path) followed by the cleaned terminal output, making it suitable for documentation, sharing, or archival purposes. LLM-Enhanced Transcripts (v0.24.0) When Ollama is running locally, CrewDeck uses a local LLM to produce an enhanced transcript with: Phased narrative sections (Initialization, Data Retrieval, Processing, etc.) with code blocks for tool invocations Token usage summary table (when visible in terminal output) ASCII session timeline Key observations list The LLM enhancement has a 3-minute timeout and gracefully falls back to the programmatic formatter if Ollama is unavailable or the LLM request fails. Input is truncated to 100 KB and output is capped at 50 KB to prevent excessive resource usage. How to Download a Transcript Open the task by clicking on its card in the Kanban board Click the Save Transcript (download icon) button in the task modal header If the task has multiple terminal sessions, a session picker appears -- select the session you want A native OS save dialog appears with a default filename based on the task number (e.g., ENG-0001-transcript.md) Choose a destination and confirm What Gets Generated ANSI escape codes are stripped to produce clean, readable output A metadata header with task number, title, execution phase, session status, start/end timestamps, duration, PR URL, branch name, worktree path, AI tool used, and command name The complete terminal output formatted as a Markdown code block (programmatic mode) or a phased narrative with structured sections (LLM-enhanced mode) A truncation notice is appended if the raw output exceeds 10 MB (Lesson #15 size limit) When to Use Transcripts vs Raw Output Format Best For Raw output (Save Output) Log analysis tools, plain-text ingestion, debugging Markdown transcript (Save Transcript) Documentation, team sharing, PR references, archival The system retrieves output from three sources in priority order, maximizing the chance of recovering complete logs: In-memory circular buffer (most complete, up to 10 MB) Ring buffer from the virtualized terminal renderer Legacy database column (fallback for older sessions) Push Notification Navigation​ Clicking a CrewDeck push notification now navigates directly to the related terminal session, eliminating the need to manually locate the correct session tab. How It Works When an agent task completes, fails, or requires user input, CrewDeck sends a system notification. Clicking the notification: Brings the CrewDeck window to the foreground (if minimized or behind other windows) Navigates to the project that owns the task Switches the Kanban board to the Board tab Opens the terminal panel and selects the relevant session tab automatically Notification Types That Support Navigation Notification Navigation Target Task completed successfully Task's terminal session (read-only, shows final output) Task failed Task's terminal session with error output visible Command approval required Task's terminal session with the approval banner focused Agent waiting for input Task's terminal session with cursor at the input prompt Session limit reached Terminal settings panel Notification Permissions Push notifications require OS-level notification permission. If you have not granted permission, CrewDeck prompts once during first launch. You can manage notification permissions in your OS system settings. System Health Monitoring​ CrewDeck monitors system CPU and memory usage to prevent new terminal sessions from being spawned when the system is overloaded. Health Status Badge A status badge appears in the terminal panel header showing the current system health: Badge Color Meaning Normal Green checkmark System is healthy; you can spawn sessions freely High Yellow warning System under pressure; consider closing sessions if you experience slowdowns Critical Red stop System overloaded; new sessions cannot be spawned Session Spawn Gating When system health reaches critical levels, CrewDeck prevents new terminal sessions from being created: An error message explains why the session was blocked (e.g., CPU or memory percentage) The message suggests how many sessions to close to free resources Warning banners also appear in the task view modal when the system is under pressure Adaptive Thresholds Thresholds become stricter as the number of active sessions increases: Active Sessions High Threshold Critical Threshold 0-9 70% 85% 10-14 65% 80% 15+ 60% 75% These thresholds apply to both CPU and memory usage independently. Note: Health status refreshes automatically every 30 seconds. If the health check itself fails, session spawning is allowed to proceed (fail-open behavior) to avoid false denials. Sleep Prevention​ CrewDeck automatically prevents your computer from going to sleep while active terminal sessions are running, ensuring long-running AI agent tasks are not interrupted. How It Works Sleep prevention activates automatically using Electron's built-in powerSaveBlocker API: Automatic activation: When the first terminal session spawns (interactive or task execution) Reference counting: Sleep prevention stays active as long as at least one session is running Automatic deactivation: When the last terminal session exits or is killed Cross-platform: Works on macOS, Windows, and Linux Blocker Type CrewDeck uses the prevent-app-suspension blocker type: System sleep: Prevented — your machine stays awake Display sleep: Allowed — your screen can turn off to save power Background operation: Enabled — sessions continue running even with display off Manual Control You don't need to manually run caffeinate or adjust system settings. Sleep prevention is fully automated based on terminal session lifecycle. Status Visibility While sleep prevention doesn't have a visible indicator in the UI, you can verify it's active by checking: System settings show the application preventing sleep macOS Activity Monitor shows CrewDeck preventing idle sleep Your system won't go to sleep automatically during active agent execution Clean Shutdown Sleep prevention is forcefully stopped when: You quit CrewDeck All terminal sessions are terminated The application is restarted App Refresh Protection​ CrewDeck prevents accidental renderer refreshes (Cmd+R, Ctrl+R, F5) when active terminal sessions exist, protecting you from losing running AI agent work and wasted Claude API tokens.
