Two-Layer Defense CrewDeck uses defense-in-depth with independent safety layers: Layer 1: Main Process Interception (Primary) Intercepts keyboard shortcuts: Cmd+R, Ctrl+R, Cmd+Shift+R, Ctrl+Shift+R, F5 Queries active terminal session count Shows a native confirmation dialog when sessions are running Dialog displays: Warning icon and session count Risk explanation (API token waste, task interruption) "Cancel" (default) and "Refresh Anyway" buttons Allows normal refresh when no sessions are active Layer 2: Renderer beforeunload Handler (Secondary) Catches edge cases like programmatic refreshes or browser-triggered navigation Checks Zustand store for running sessions Calls preventDefault() to trigger browser warning prompt Only activates when running sessions exist User Experience Scenario Behavior Cmd+R with 0 sessions Refreshes normally without prompt Cmd+R with 1+ sessions Native dialog shows warning, blocks refresh by default User clicks "Cancel" Page stays loaded, sessions continue running User clicks "Refresh Anyway" Page reloads (explicit confirmation) F12, Zoom shortcuts Still work normally (not intercepted) Why This Matters Accidental refreshes during AI agent execution: Destroy WebContents sender references, orphaning PTY sessions Waste Claude API tokens from interrupted mid-task processing Lose session state (although reconnection exists as a safety net) Terminal Sandboxing As of v0.13.0, all renderer windows run in Electron sandbox mode (sandbox: true). Refresh protection now also accounts for the sandboxed renderer context: if the renderer is compromised or in an unexpected state, the main-process interception layer (Layer 1) continues to function independently, maintaining protection even when the renderer beforeunload handler cannot fire. Dialog Behavior Only one dialog shown at a time (prevents stacking from rapid key presses) Native dialog blocks event loop (appropriate for critical confirmation) Works even if renderer is in a bad state Session count checked at time of keypress (TOCTOU consideration: if sessions complete while dialog is open, refreshing is harmless)

CrewDeck automates the creation and management of Pull Requests. Draft PRs​ When a task starts execution: A draft PR is created immediately after the branch is pushed Draft PRs are marked as "Draft" on GitHub This allows work-in-progress to be visible without triggering CI/CD pipelines Viewing PRs​ Once a PR is created: The task card displays a PR link (looks like a chain icon or "PR" label) Click the link to open the PR on GitHub The PR title includes the task title and task number Review Status​ Task Status PR State In Progress Draft PR In Review Ready for Review Done (Depends on GitHub merge status) Completing a Task​ After reviewing and merging the PR: Drag the task to the Done column The task is marked as completed The worktree can be cleaned up (manual process) GitHub Issue Auto-Close (v0.11.0) When a task with a linked GitHub Issue is marked as complete: The associated GitHub Issue is automatically closed A comment is added to the issue with a link to the merged Pull Request This ensures issue tracking stays synchronized with task completion No manual intervention required PR Watcher​ The PR Watcher scans a project's open pull requests on a schedule, auto-merges the eligible ones and dispatches fix agents for failing checks. Its settings live in Settings → Autonomy → PR Watcher; the poll-mode controls appear once the watcher is enabled for the project. Poll modes Mode What drives scans Poll (default) An interval scan every 5 minutes (or the project's configured interval, never faster than 30 seconds) Hybrid Webhook deliveries, plus a reconcile scan at most every 6 hours — only while the project has an active webhook subscription Webhook Webhook deliveries only, with no interval scan — only while the project has an active webhook subscription Fallback rule. Hybrid and Webhook need an active webhook subscription for the project's primary repository. Until one exists, both modes fall back to polling at the configured interval, exactly like Poll mode. The 6-hour reconcile floor and the timer-less webhook mode apply only while a subscription is active. Hybrid and Webhook also fall back to polling while this desktop is signed out of CrewDeck Cloud, or signed in on a plan without PR Watcher. Enabling webhook delivery. Sign in to CrewDeck Cloud (Settings → Cloud Sync). Be on a plan that includes PR Watcher: trial, Pro or Founder. Choose Hybrid or Webhook in Settings → Autonomy → PR Watcher. The relay section appears only for those two modes. CrewDeck creates the GitHub webhook on the project's primary repository itself. There is no URL or token to enter. If this desktop is signed out, the relay section shows "Sign in to CrewDeck Cloud to receive PR Watcher webhooks." with a Sign in button. If your plan does not include the feature, it shows "PR Watcher webhooks aren't included in your plan" instead. Relay status. A status pill shows the connection to CrewDeck's webhook relay: Status Meaning Connected (green) Deliveries arrive within seconds. Connecting / Reconnecting (amber, pulsing) The relay connection is opening or re-opening. Deliveries made meanwhile are queued and replayed on reconnect, each processed once. Error (red) The connection failed; the reason is shown next to the pill. Disconnected (grey) No relay connection. Delivery URL and Reset URL. The relay section shows this desktop's delivery URL read-only ("Delivery URL not issued yet" until the relay has issued one). Reset URL issues a new delivery URL; the old one keeps working for 24 hours, and the GitHub webhooks are repointed automatically. When the button is disabled, the reason is shown beside it: "Resetting the delivery URL…", "Available once the relay is connected." or "Available once the relay has issued a delivery URL." Caution: the delivery URL is a capability: anyone who has it can post deliveries to this desktop. Do not paste it publicly, and reset it if it leaks. While signed out. The GitHub webhooks stay registered. Deliveries queue in the cloud for up to 7 days (up to 500 per desktop) and are replayed after the same account signs back in. Privacy. GitHub webhook payloads pass through, and are briefly stored encrypted in, CrewDeck's cloud relay. They are deleted on acknowledgement or after 7 days. Seeing the real cadence. Under the poll-mode selector, an effective-interval line shows what the watcher is actually doing, e.g. "Scanning every 5m", "Scanning every 5m (interval fallback)" or "Webhook-driven; reconcile scan every 6h". When a webhook mode is running on its fallback, an amber warning explains why and which interval is in use instead: "Sign in to CrewDeck Cloud to receive PR Watcher webhooks. The watcher is polling every 5m instead." "Your plan does not include PR Watcher webhooks. The watcher is polling every 5m instead." "Webhook delivery is unavailable (reason). The watcher is polling every 5m instead." "No active webhook subscription for this project's primary repository. The watcher is polling every 5m instead." If auto-merge seems slow. Builds released before this fallback existed created new projects in Hybrid mode and scanned them only every 6 hours. Builds that include the fallback correct this automatically. On an older build, switch the project to Poll and trigger a scan from the developer console: await window.api.prWatcher.updateSettings('<projectId>', { pollMode: 'poll' }) await window.api.prWatcher.runScanNow('<projectId>') On macOS, open the developer console with View → Toggle Developer Tools. Packaged Windows and Linux builds have no application menu, so this workaround may not be reachable there.

Create versioned releases of completed work with automated documentation and PR workflows. Creating a Release​ Navigate to your project Ensure you have tasks in the "Done" column Click the New Release button (visible when done tasks exist) Enter a version number (format: 1.2.3) The system suggests the next version based on previous releases Use semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH Select which "Done" tasks to include in this release Click Create Release What Happens During Release Creation​ The release workflow executes automatically: Phase What Happens 1. Worktree Creation Creates isolated git worktree for release branch 2. Branch Creation Creates branch named release/YYYY-MM-DD-xxxxxx 3. Manifest Generation Creates .release-manifest.json with version and task info 4. Documentation Claude CLI runs /do-release command to generate release notes 5. Commit Changes are committed to the release branch 6. Push Branch is pushed to GitHub 7. PR Creation Pull request is opened for the release 8. Task Archival Included tasks are marked as released Release Documentation​ The /do-release command automatically: Creates docs/release/v{version}.md with release notes Archives prompts to prompts/archived/ Updates CHANGELOG.md Organizes task information by category Viewing Release History​ Navigate to your project Click the Releases tab View all releases with: Version number Status (pending, in_progress, completed, failed) Number of included tasks Creation date Click View to see release details and included tasks Release Status​ Status Description Pending Release created, waiting to start In Progress Release workflow is executing Completed Release PR successfully created Failed Release workflow encountered an error Terminal Output​ The release creation process displays real-time output in the terminal panel, showing each phase as it executes. You can monitor progress and see any errors that occur during the workflow. Releases, Release Notes and Podcasts​ The Review → Releases page is the single place for every kind of release: the Major/Minor releases you cut with the release wizard, the hotfixes ingested from GitHub, their release notes, and their audio podcasts. Note: Release Notes used to be a separate page. It has been merged into Releases. Existing ?tab=release-notes links still work — they now open the Releases page. Accessing Releases Open a project and navigate to Review → Releases The table lists each release with its Version, Status, Branch, Created and Released dates, Total Cost, PR link, and per-row actions Showing hotfixes By default the table lists only Major/Minor releases — the X.Y.0 versions the release wizard produces. Click Include Hotfixes in the page header to add patch releases (X.Y.Z where Z is not zero — in practice the releases ingested from GitHub) Click it again to hide them Hotfix rows show a Hotfix badge, and leave Branch, Total Cost and PR blank — those fields have no meaning for a release that was published on GitHub rather than cut through a CrewDeck pull request Viewing release-note details Click the chevron beside any version to expand that release in place. The detail row shows the release title, the tag name, the full release-notes body, the audio file path and duration when a podcast exists, and a View on GitHub button for releases that have a GitHub page. Syncing releases from GitHub Click Ingest releases in the page header to fetch the latest releases from GitHub Requires a primary repository to be connected Syncs release metadata including title, version tag, and GitHub URL This is the only way hotfix rows appear, so run it before turning on Include Hotfixes on a project you have not synced Generating and playing release podcasts Each released row carries a single microphone icon whose colour tells you what clicking it will do: Icon Meaning Clicking it Green A playable audio file exists on disk Opens the file in your system's default audio player Gray No audio file, or the file is gone Generates the podcast Spinner Generation is in progress Disabled; shows the current phase Generating requires the release_podcasts_folder setting to be configured. If the file was deleted or the output folder was repointed, the icon returns to gray with an "Audio missing" hint so you can regenerate it. For bulk operations, use the Generate missing button in the page header: Click Generate missing The system processes up to 25 releases per invocation Already-generated releases are skipped Failed releases are reported without stopping the batch If more releases remain, the UI prompts you to run the batch again PR Review with Inline Diff Viewer​ CrewDeck provides an integrated code review experience with inline diff visualization and AI-detected findings. Viewing PR Diffs​ When reviewing a Pull Request: Click the Review button on the task card The inline diff viewer opens, displaying: File list — All changed files with diff hunks Line numbers — Original and new line numbers for added/removed code Syntax highlighting — Color-coded diffs for readability Findings panel — AI-detected issues (security, performance, style) Understanding Findings​ AI agents automatically detect and annotate findings in the diff: Severity Color Meaning Critical Red Security or major correctness issue High Orange Performance or design concern Medium Yellow Code quality or maintainability issue Low Blue Minor style or naming suggestion Each finding displays: Title — Brief description of the issue Category — Type of finding (Security, Performance, Style, etc.) Line number — Exact location in the code Description — Detailed explanation on hover or expand Review Actions​ For each finding, you can: Action Purpose Accept Acknowledge the finding and keep it in the summary Dismiss Discard the finding (won't appear in summary) Expand View the full description and context Review Summary Panel​ At the top of the diff viewer: Finding breakdown — Count of findings by severity level Category distribution — Findings grouped by type (Security, Performance, Style, etc.) Dismissed count — Number of dismissed findings Filter controls — Multi-select filters for severity and category (future enhancement) Completing a Review​ After reviewing the diff: Address any critical findings by requesting changes or updates Click Complete Review to finish The review status updates on GitHub Merge the PR when all findings are resolved

When a task reaches the "Document" column on the Kanban board, CrewDeck provides a structured wizard-style interface for generating documentation, rather than requiring raw terminal interaction. Using the Document Wizard​ Locate a task in the Document column Click the Run button on the task card The Document Wizard modal opens instead of the terminal Wizard Steps​ Step Name Description 1 Confirm Review task details, PR link, and the documentation workflow description before proceeding 2 Execute Watch animated progress as documentation is generated, committed, and pushed 3 Complete View success message and click "View Pull Request" to see the result on GitHub Documentation Phases​ During execution, the wizard tracks three phases with visual status indicators: Phase Description Generating documentation AI generates documentation based on the task context Committing changes Documentation files are committed to the feature branch Pushing to remote Changes are pushed to GitHub Each phase shows a status icon (pending, in progress, completed, or failed) that updates in real time. Error Handling​ If documentation generation fails: The wizard displays an error message with details A Retry button allows you to attempt the workflow again The terminal session continues running in the background and remains accessible from the terminal panel

The Agents, Commands and Skills tabs let you manage Claude Code configurations directly from CrewDeck. You can add, generate, and remove agents, skills, and commands for your connected repositories. Agents, Commands and Skills Tabs Overview​ The three tabs appear under Crew in the project header when at least one repository is connected. Each shows one configuration type, with the same interface and the same actions. Accessing the Tabs Navigate to your project Open the Build dropdown in the project header Choose Agents, Commands or Skills (visible only when repositories are connected) Configuration Cards Each configuration item is displayed as a card showing: Element Description Type Badge Indicates whether it's an agent, command, or skill Category The functional category (e.g., "Development", "Testing") Model The AI model used (for agents, e.g., "sonnet", "opus") Title The name of the configuration Description A brief explanation of what it does File Path The location in the repository Config Panel Layout Adding from Templates​ Templates are pre-built configurations that provide common agents, skills, and commands. Use them to quickly set up your repository with proven configurations. Opening the Template Selector Navigate to your project's Crew → Agents, Commands or Skills tab Click the Add from Templates button in the top-right corner The Template Selector modal opens Using the Template Selector Step Action 1 Browse available templates organized by type (Agents, Commands, Skills) 2 Use the search bar to find specific templates by name or description 3 Filter by type using the tab navigation 4 Click on templates to select them (a checkmark appears) 5 Click again to deselect 6 Review your selections in the summary area 7 Click Add X Templates to proceed What Happens Next When you add templates: CrewDeck generates the configuration files A new branch is created in your repository The files are committed to the branch A Pull Request is created for review You can review and merge the PR on GitHub Generating New Configurations​ The Generate wizard uses AI to create custom configurations based on your description. This is useful when templates don't match your specific needs. Opening the Generate Wizard Navigate to your project's Crew → Agents, Commands or Skills tab Click the Generate button in the top-right corner The Generate Config Wizard opens The 4-Step Generation Process Step Name What You Do 1 Describe Enter a natural language description of what you need 2 Select Types Choose what to generate: Agents, Skills, and/or Commands 3 Review Review AI-generated suggestions, select or deselect items 4 Complete Confirm and create a PR with the selected configurations Step 1: Describe Write a clear description of the configurations you need. For example: "I need agents for React development and code review" "Create a skill for deploying to AWS with automated testing" "Generate commands for database migrations and API testing" Step 2: Select Types Choose which types of configurations to generate: Type Use Case Agents Specialized AI assistants for specific tasks (e.g., frontend-developer, database-designer) Skills Reusable workflows invoked with slash commands (e.g., /commit, /review-pr) Commands Task automation scripts (e.g., /build-feature, /fix-bug) Step 3: Review The AI generates suggested configurations based on your description: Each suggestion shows name, description, and type Click to select/deselect individual items Review carefully before proceeding You can go back to modify your description if needed Step 4: Complete After confirmation: Selected configurations are generated as files A feature branch is created Files are committed to the branch A Pull Request is created on GitHub A link to the PR is displayed Removing Configurations​ You can remove configurations that are no longer needed directly from these tabs. Removing a Configuration Navigate to the Crew → Agents, Commands or Skills tab Find the configuration card you want to remove Hover over the card to reveal the Remove button (trash icon) Click the Remove button Confirm the removal in the dialog What Happens When you remove a configuration: A new branch is created in your repository The configuration file is deleted The change is committed A Pull Request is created for review Once merged, the configuration is removed from the repository Note: Removing a configuration doesn't immediately delete it. The PR must be merged on GitHub for the removal to take effect.

When you connect a new repository that doesn't have Claude configurations, CrewDeck offers an onboarding wizard to help you set up agents, skills, and commands quickly. When the Wizard Appears​ The onboarding wizard appears when: A repository is first connected to a project The repository lacks existing .claude/ configuration directories You haven't previously dismissed the wizard for this repository Wizard Steps​ Step Name Description 1 Agents Select pre-built agents to import (e.g., frontend-developer, code-reviewer) 2 Skills Select skills to import (e.g., commit, review-pr, build-feature) 3 Commands Select commands to import (e.g., /fix-bug, /create-pr) 4 Confirm Review your selections and create the PR Using the Wizard​ Step 1: Select Agents Browse available agent templates Check the agents you want to add Each agent shows its name, description, and capabilities Click Next to continue Step 2: Select Skills Browse available skill templates Check the skills you want to add Skills are reusable workflows like /commit or /review-pr Click Next to continue Step 3: Select Commands Browse available command templates Check the commands you want to add Commands are task-specific automations Click Next to continue Step 4: Confirm Review all selected configurations See a summary of what will be created Click Create PR to proceed After Completion Configuration files are generated in the repository A feature branch is created A Pull Request is opened on GitHub Merge the PR to activate the configurations Sync the repository to see the new configurations in CrewDeck Skipping the Wizard​ If you prefer to set up configurations manually or later: Click Skip or Later to dismiss the wizard You can always use the Add from Templates or Generate features on the Agents, Commands and Skills tabs later

The "Build With Me" feature guides you through creating a new project from scratch using AI-powered collaboration. This multi-stage wizard walks you through project definition, technology selection, architecture design, and roadmap generation. Accessing Build With Me​ Navigate to your project page Open the Build With Me tab (the only place sessions are started, so the session is always scoped to the project you are viewing) Click Start — enabled once the project has a connected primary repository and no session is already running A wizard modal opens with the project creation flow The Five Stages​ Stage 1: Project Description Describe your project in natural language: Type your project vision, goals, and key features The AI assistant asks clarifying questions Continue the conversation until you feel the project is well-defined Click Next to proceed to technology selection Stage 2: Tech Stack Debate Review AI-recommended technology stacks: The AI agent presents multiple technology options (Frontend frameworks, backends, databases, etc.) Each option shows: Suitability Score (0-100) indicating how well it fits your project Pros — Advantages of this choice Cons — Potential drawbacks Select your preferred tech stack Click Approve to confirm and proceed Stage 3: Architecture Proposal Review the AI-generated architecture design: See detailed system architecture diagrams and component descriptions Review technology integration patterns Two action options: Approve — Accept the architecture and move to scaffold generation Request Changes — Provide feedback for the AI to refine the design Stage 4: Scaffold Generation Review the initial project scaffold: View the proposed file structure and directory layout See template configurations and boilerplate code Review for correctness and completeness Approve or request changes Stage 5: Roadmap Kickoff View the AI-generated project roadmap: See milestone-based breakdown of implementation phases Review feature priorities and dependencies Understand timeline and effort estimates Click Complete to finish the wizard Review Completed Stages​ As you progress through the wizard, completed stages appear above the active stage: Click to expand and view previous stage outputs Review decisions and generated content anytime Provides a narrative of how the project evolved Error Handling​ If an error occurs during the session: An error banner appears with details Click Dismiss to close the error message Fix any issues (e.g., network connectivity) and Retry Your session state is preserved for recovery What Happens After Completion​ After completing the wizard: The project scaffold is generated Initial files are created in your connected repository A feature branch is created for the project setup A Pull Request is opened on GitHub You can review, adjust, and merge the PR to activate your new project

CrewDeck is built around Claude Code as the primary AI coding assistant. While the architecture supports multiple AI tools, Claude Code provides the deepest integration with features like Agent Teams, task coordination, and advanced execution modes. Claude Code (Primary)​ Claude Code is the recommended and primary AI coding tool for CrewDeck with full feature support: Feature Support CLI Command claude Model Selection Sonnet (default), Opus, Haiku Execution Modes Sequential, Swarm, and Team modes Agent Teams Full support for independent teammate spawning Session Resume Pause and resume capability with session persistence Permission System Three-tier permission hook (fast approve, fast deny, LLM analysis) via @abdo-el-mobayad/claude-code-fast-permission-hook Installing Claude Code npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code Model Selection CrewDeck supports all Claude Code models: Model Best For Context Window Opus Complex tasks requiring deep reasoning and multi-step planning Large Sonnet (default) Balanced performance and speed for most tasks Medium Haiku Quick tasks, faster responses, lower token usage Small Other AI Tools (Limited Support)​ While CrewDeck's architecture includes support for other AI coding tools, these are considered legacy with limited feature sets: Tool CLI Command Status Limitations Cursor cursor Legacy No Agent Teams, no pause/resume, limited execution modes Gemini CLI gemini Legacy No Agent Teams, no pause/resume, limited execution modes GitHub Copilot gh copilot Legacy Basic CLI integration only Note: Team execution mode, pause/resume, and Agent Teams features require Claude Code and will not work with other tools. Configuring AI Tools​ Accessing AI Tool Settings Click Settings in the sidebar (gear icon) Scroll to the AI Coding Tools section You'll see all registered AI tools with their availability status Detecting Installed Tools Click the Detect Tools button CrewDeck scans your system for installed AI coding tools Available tools are marked with a green checkmark Unavailable tools are grayed out with installation instructions Setting a Default Tool Find the AI tool you want to use as default Click Set as Default on that tool's card The tool is now used for all task executions (unless overridden) Selecting a Model For tools that support multiple models (like Claude Code): Find the tool card Use the Model dropdown to select your preferred model Models affect capabilities, speed, and token usage Model Best For Opus Complex tasks requiring deep reasoning Sonnet Balanced performance and speed Haiku Quick tasks, lower token usage LLM Chat Model and Embeddings (Ollama)​ CrewDeck uses Ollama for all local AI features — chat summaries, task embeddings for semantic search, and agent recommendations. No external API keys are required for these capabilities. Default Models Function Model Notes Chat / Summaries qwen3:8b Used for daily activity summaries and AI-powered analysis Task Embeddings nomic-embed-text 768-dimensional local embeddings for semantic search Setup Install Ollama on your machine Pull the required models: ollama pull qwen3:8b ollama pull nomic-embed-text Start Ollama (ollama serve or via the Ollama desktop app) CrewDeck automatically connects to http://127.0.0.1:11434 What Uses Ollama Feature Model Used AI Daily Activity Summary qwen3:8b (falls back to structured plaintext if unavailable) Task Intelligence (semantic search) nomic-embed-text Intelligent Agent Recommendations nomic-embed-text Note: Ollama is optional. If it is not running, AI features fall back to simpler non-AI alternatives. Core task execution with Claude Code does not require Ollama. Per-Task Tool Selection​ When enabled, you can select different AI tools for individual tasks: Enabling Per-Task Override Go to Settings > AI Coding Tools Enable Allow per-task tool selection Optionally enable Allow per-task model selection Selecting Tool When Creating a Task Open the Create Task modal In the AI Tool dropdown, select your preferred tool Optionally select a specific model The task will use the selected tool during execution Note: If a task doesn't have a tool selected, it uses the project's default or global default.

Browse and install pre-built agents, commands, skills, and hooks from the marketplace to quickly expand your project's capabilities. New in v0.15.0: The marketplace now supports four item types — agents, commands, skills, and hooks. You can filter the marketplace by type to find exactly what you need.
Navigate to your project Click the Agents tab Click the Browse Marketplace button Browse available items by type or category

Click on an item card to view details Review the item's description, capabilities, and version Click Install or Update (if a newer version is available) Select the target repository for installation For established repositories (2+ commits): A feature branch is created The item file is added to the appropriate .claude/ subdirectory A Pull Request is opened for review Review and merge the PR on GitHub For new repositories (0-1 commits): The item is committed directly to the default branch Sync your repository to see the new item in your project
Navigate to the Agents tab Find the installed marketplace item Click Uninstall in the item detail modal A PR is created to remove the item file Review and merge the PR on GitHub

Browse items by type (agents, commands, skills, hooks) and category (development, testing, documentation, etc.) Filter by item type to narrow results to what you need View ratings and usage statistics for each item Filter and search items by name or capability Track installation status (installed, pending PR, updates available) Marketplace Item Types (v0.15.0) Type Description Installed To Agent AI specialist that executes tasks (e.g., frontend-developer) .claude/agents/ Command Slash command defining a specific workflow (e.g., /build-feature) .claude/commands/ Skill Reusable workflow automation extending Claude's capabilities .claude/skills/ Hook Automation triggered by lifecycle events (e.g., on task complete) .claude/hooks/

As of v0.13.0, marketplace agents declare a set of capabilities in their manifest. CrewDeck enforces these declarations to constrain what each agent is permitted to do during task execution. How Capabilities Work Each agent manifest includes a capabilities array: # .claude/agents/frontend-developer.yml name: frontend-developer capabilities: - file:read - file:write - shell:run-tests - github:create-pr When an agent attempts an action not listed in its capabilities, the operation is blocked and the agent receives an error response. This limits the blast radius if an agent behaves unexpectedly or is compromised. Standard Capability Categories Category Capabilities Description File file:read, file:write, file:delete Access to the local filesystem within the worktree Shell shell:run-tests, shell:build, shell:arbitrary Permitted shell command categories GitHub github:create-pr, github:merge-pr, github:create-issue GitHub API operations Network network:http-get, network:http-post Outbound network requests Terminal terminal:interactive, terminal:batch PTY session types Viewing Agent Capabilities Open an agent's detail card in the Agents tab to see its declared capabilities. A warning badge appears if the agent requests shell:arbitrary, which grants broad shell access. Overriding Capabilities Project administrators can expand or restrict an agent's capabilities for their project without modifying the shared agent manifest: Navigate to Agents tab and open an agent Click Customize Permissions Toggle individual capabilities on or off Click Save — overrides are stored in the project database and apply only to this project

The Living Roadmap provides a dynamic, AI-powered view of your project's development timeline. Organize work into milestones, visualize dependencies, estimate effort, and get intelligent prioritization suggestions. Accessing the Roadmap​ Navigate to your project page Click the Roadmap tab The Living Roadmap visualization appears, showing: Milestone groups (collapsed/expandable) Individual items with effort and risk indicators Dependency connections between items Status filters and sorting controls Understanding the Visualization​ Items Display Each roadmap item shows: Element Meaning Title Item name or description Priority Badge Color-coded priority (Critical/High/Medium/Low) Effort Estimate Size badge (XS, Small, Medium, Large, XL) Risk Level Risk indicator (Low/Medium/High/Critical) Dependency Count Number of items that depend on this one Linked Tasks Count of CrewDeck tasks connected to this item Milestone Groups Items are organized by milestone: Ungrouped section — Items without an assigned milestone Named milestones — Sections for each unique milestone value Collapse/expand — Click to hide/show items in each milestone Dependency Arrows Visual connections show dependencies between items: Arrow direction — Points from dependent item to the item it depends on Highlight — Cyclic dependencies (circular dependencies) are highlighted in red Routing — Arrows route around items to minimize crossing when possible Filtering and Sorting​ Status Filters Use the filter pills to show/hide items by criteria: Filter Type Options Priority Critical, High, Medium, Low Risk Level Critical, High, Medium, Low Effort XS, Small, Medium, Large, XL Click a filter to toggle visibility Multiple selections show all matching items Badge counts update to reflect current view Sorting Future enhancements will support sorting by: Priority Effort estimate Risk level Dependency count Reordering Items​ Drag items within a milestone to reorder: Click and hold an item Drag it up/down within the same milestone Drop to confirm the new position Position change is saved automatically Note: Drag-to-reorder works within milestones — items stay in their assigned milestone. AI-Powered Reprioritization​ Get intelligent priority suggestions based on dependencies, effort, and risk: Click AI Reprioritize button at the top of the roadmap The system analyzes: Dependency relationships Effort estimates Risk levels Milestone alignment Suggestions appear with: Suggested Priority — The recommended new priority level Score (0-100) — Confidence in the suggestion Reasoning — Explanation for the change (e.g., "High effort with critical dependencies") Accepting Suggestions Accept individual — Click the check icon on a suggestion to apply it Bulk accept — Click Accept All to apply all suggestions at once Dismiss — Click the X to discard a suggestion without applying it Linking Tasks​ Connect CrewDeck tasks to roadmap items: Click an item to view details Click Link Task button Select from available tasks in the project The task count badge updates View all linked tasks: Click the task count badge on an item A modal shows all linked tasks with their status and priority Risk Management​ Use risk indicators to identify high-impact items: Risk Levels Level Color Meaning Low Green Well-understood, limited technical risk Medium Yellow Some complexity or unknowns High Orange Significant complexity or external dependencies Critical Red Major technical challenges or blockers Risk Mitigation High-risk items with high effort → Plan detailed spike or POC first Critical-risk items → Schedule early in the timeline Dependent on critical items → May need to reorder (see AI Reprioritization) Effort Estimation​ Estimate implementation effort using the five-point scale: Estimate Size Time Use When XS Extra Small < 1 hour Trivial bug fixes, minor config changes Small Small 1–2 hours Simple features, straightforward tasks Medium Medium 2–8 hours Standard features, moderate complexity Large Large 1–3 days Complex features, multiple components XL Extra Large 3+ days Major subsystems, foundational architecture Dependency Management​ Adding Dependencies Click on an item to open details In the Dependencies section, click Add Dependency Select the item(s) this item depends on Confirm to save Cyclic Dependencies Items with circular dependencies are marked with a warning icon: The roadmap identifies all items involved in cycles Cyclic items cannot be properly ordered Resolution: Break the cycle by changing one dependency Topological Ordering The roadmap automatically calculates dependency order: Items with no dependencies (roots) appear first in timeline lanes Dependent items appear after their dependencies Cyclic items are flagged for manual resolution Backlog Shelf and Cycle Planning​ The Backlog Shelf provides a drag-and-drop planning interface for moving work from the backlog into cycles based on readiness and capacity. Accessing the Backlog Shelf Navigate to your project's Roadmap tab The Backlog Shelf appears as a dedicated section showing unassigned items Active cycles display as drop zones alongside the backlog Planning Items into Cycles Drag a backlog item to a cycle drop zone Alternatively, select an item and use keyboard shortcuts to move it The system validates: Readiness: Item has no blocking dependencies Capacity: Cycle has remaining budget for the item's effort estimate If validation fails, inline hints explain why the item can't be moved Once accepted, the item updates its cycle assignment and appears in the cycle view Capacity Tracking Each cycle displays: Committed: Total effort allocated to the cycle Burned: Effort consumed by completed work Remaining: Budget still available for new work Visual indicators showing cycle fill level Cycle Ledger: Committed vs Burned​ The Cycle Ledger view provides financial tracking for work planned and executed within a cycle. Accessing the Cycle Ledger Navigate to your project's Roadmap tab Click the Cycle Ledger button The ledger displays all cycles with committed and burned metrics Ledger Columns Column Description Cycle Name Name or identifier of the planning cycle Committed Total dollar value allocated to work in this cycle Burned Actual dollar value consumed by completed work Remaining Budget still available (Committed - Burned) Utilization Percentage of budget used (Burned / Committed × 100%) asOf Freshness timestamp of the ledger data Using the Ledger Identify cycles running over budget (Burned > Committed) Plan work allocation for upcoming cycles based on historical burn rates Monitor project spend against planned budgets Make forecasting adjustments based on utilization trends Freshness Contract The "asOf" timestamp indicates when the data was last calculated: Refreshed automatically on cycle changes or work completion Manual refresh available to force recalculation Staleness warning appears if data is older than 1 hour Product Requirements Document (PRD) Handling (v0.71.0)​ PRD (Product Requirements Document) handling enables structured parsing and management of product specifications, with intelligent requirement extraction and backlog integration. PRD Document Organization Document sections: PRD documents are organized into named sections (e.g., Overview, Features, Success Criteria). Each section can be independently edited, parsed, and grilled for requirements. Requirement capture: Use the PRD Grilling feature to extract structured requirements from each section. Requirements are parsed by section, enabling fine-grained requirement-to-backlog traceability. Mockups page: The PRD includes a mockups section for visual specification with restyle options to improve layout clarity. Creating Requirements from PRD Sections Author or upload a PRD document to a project The system parses the document into named sections For each section, use the Grill action to run AI-powered requirement extraction Extracted requirements are displayed by section with full context Promote requirements to backlog items with one click, automatically linking them to the source PRD section PRD-to-Backlog Workflow Once requirements are grilled from a PRD: Review extracted requirements grouped by section Select one or more requirements to promote to backlog items Each promoted item retains a link to its source PRD section Backlog items show section context in their detail panel When promoting backlog items to the Kanban board, requirement traceability flows through to created tasks

The Execution Replay Service captures complete snapshots of task executions, allowing you to review, compare, and analyze past runs for debugging and learning purposes. What Gets Captured Each execution snapshot includes: Terminal output: Last 512KB of terminal logs (tail-truncated for large outputs) Agent traces: All agent decision events, tool usage, and phase transitions Command steps: Status, duration, and outcomes of each command in a chain Task outcome: Success/failure status and error messages Metadata: Execution timestamp, task details, agent names Capturing a Snapshot Snapshots are captured automatically when task execution completes (success or failure). You can also manually trigger a snapshot: Navigate to a completed task Click Capture Snapshot in the task detail view The snapshot is saved to the database Viewing Execution History To view all snapshots for a task: Open the task detail view Navigate to the Execution History tab See a list of all execution attempts with timestamps and outcomes Comparing Executions Compare two different executions of the same task to understand what changed: In the Execution History tab, select two snapshots Click Compare The comparison view shows: Terminal Diff Jaccard similarity score between terminal outputs Indicates how similar the execution logs were Agent Trace Diff Phase sequence comparison (which phases ran in each execution) Event count distribution across phases Identifies where agents spent time differently Command Step Diff Side-by-side status comparison for each command step Duration differences (which steps took longer/shorter) Identifies which steps succeeded vs. failed in each run Outcome Diff Success/failure status changes Duration comparison Error message differences Use Cases Debugging failures: Compare a failed run to a successful one to identify what went wrong Performance analysis: See which execution was faster and why Agent behavior: Understand how different agent configurations affect outcomes Regression detection: Identify when and how execution behavior changed

Share releases and activity summaries with your team via Git, enabling collaboration and visibility across team members. How It Works Team data is exported as JSON files to a .crewdeck/shared/ directory in your project's primary repository: releases.json: Last 10 releases with task links activity-summaries.json: Last 30 daily activity summaries These files are tracked in Git alongside your code, providing clean diffs and version history. Exporting Team Data Manual export: Navigate to Settings → Team Data Click Export Releases or Export Summaries Files are written to .crewdeck/shared/ in your primary repository Commit and push the changes to share with teammates Automatic export: Releases are automatically exported when you create a new release Activity summaries are automatically exported when generated The "Auto-export" setting (enabled by default) controls this behavior Importing Team Data When teammates pull the repository with shared data: Navigate to Settings → Team Data Click Import Team Data The system reads .crewdeck/shared/*.json files

Export collaboration data (releases, activity summaries, project data) into a GitHub draft pull request using git worktrees, providing a reviewable, version-controlled export path without modifying your working tree. How It Works The export-to-PR workflow uses git worktrees to create deterministic exports: Fetch Latest: Pulls latest changes from remote repository Default Branch Detection: Automatically detects default branch (main/master) using three-tier fallback Temporary Worktree: Creates a temporary git worktree with unique branch (export/<type>-YYYY-MM-DD-<nanoid>) File Export: Writes export files to .crewdeck/shared/export/ directory via callback Commit & Push: Stages, commits, and pushes changes automatically Draft PR Creation: Creates a draft PR via gh CLI Cleanup: Removes the temporary worktree (with fallback to force-delete + prune) Available Export Types Export Type Data Included Access Point Project Data Tasks, agents, commands, configurations Settings → Data Export Team Releases Last 10 releases with task links Settings → Team Data Activity Summaries Last 30 daily activity summaries Settings → Team Data Exporting to PR Navigate to Settings → Data Export or Team Data Click the green Export to PR button for your desired export type Wait for the export process (~10-30 seconds depending on repository size) A success message displays the PR URL Click the PR URL link to open it in your default browser Review the exported files in the PR diff Merge the PR when ready to share with your team Export File Structure All exports write to .crewdeck/shared/export/: project-data.json or project-data.yaml: Full project export releases.json: Team releases activity-summaries.json: Daily activity summaries PR Details Created draft PRs include: Title: Descriptive export type and timestamp Branch Name: export/<type>-YYYY-MM-DD-<unique-id> Status: Draft (requires review before merge) Commit Message: Automated message indicating export source Body: Summary of exported data Why Worktrees? Using git worktree add instead of direct file writes provides: Complete isolation from your current work No risk of conflicts with uncommitted changes No need for git stashing Atomic operation — if anything fails, your repo is untouched Requirements Git: Standard git installation gh CLI: Must be installed and authenticated # Install gh CLI brew install gh # macOS # or download from https://cli.github.com # Authenticate gh auth login GitHub Token: Must have repo scope with push permissions Primary Repository: Project must have a connected primary repository Error Handling Error Cause Solution gh CLI not found gh CLI not installed or not in PATH Install gh CLI and authenticate Git fetch failed Network error or invalid repository Check internet connection, verify repository exists Worktree creation failed Worktree path conflict Previous worktree cleanup issue — manually delete stale worktree PR creation failed GitHub API error or permissions Check token has push access, verify repository isn't archived Opening PR URLs After a successful export: The PR URL is displayed in a green highlight box Click the URL to open it in your default browser using shell.openExternal() The URL is also logged to the terminal for copy/paste Security All git commands use spawnSync with array arguments (no shell injection) Command inputs are hardcoded strings (not user-controlled) Worktree paths use app.getPath('userData') (application-controlled location) Timeouts prevent hangs: 30s for git operations, 60s for gh CLI

CrewDeck automatically learns from completed task executions and enriches new task prompts with relevant historical patterns, enabling AI agents to improve over time. How It Works Cross-task learning operates in two phases: Phase 1: Extraction (on task completion) When a task transitions to "done" status: Fetches task details, outcome, agents, commands, and terminal output Builds structured patterns (agent configuration, command sequences, execution mode, duration) Extracts error/resolution pairs from terminal output via regex heuristics Extracts key decisions from agent trace events Calculates a quality score (0-100) based on outcome status, user rating, and error count Stores the learning with upsert semantics (one learning per task) Ensures an embedding exists for semantic similarity matching Phase 2: Injection (before task execution) When a task is about to execute: Checks if cross-task learning is enabled (feature flag in settings) Uses 500ms timeout-protected query to fetch relevant learnings Finds semantically similar tasks via TaskIntelligenceService Filters learnings by project scope, minimum similarity (0.4), and minimum quality (30) Formats top 3 learnings as markdown with agent config, commands, errors, decisions, and outcome Appends the formatted context to the task description before passing to AI agent Learning Data Structure Each learning captures: Field Description Patterns Agent IDs/names, command info, execution mode, duration, outcome status Error Resolutions Error/resolution pairs extracted from terminal output (max 10 pairs) Key Decisions Decisions from agent trace events (description, phase, confidence) Output Summary Truncated terminal output (max 10KB) with priority retention (first 20% + last 80%) Quality Score 0-100 score based on outcome, user rating, and error count Quality Scoring Algorithm Base score: success → 80 partial → 50 failure → 20 unknown → 20 User rating bonus (if rated 1-5): bonus = (rating - 3) * 5 // Range: -10 to +10 Error penalty: penalty = min(10, errorCount * 2) Final = clamp(base + bonus - penalty, 0, 100) Enabling Cross-Task Learning Navigate to Settings → Advanced → Cross-Task Learning Toggle the Enable Cross-Task Learning switch Learnings are extracted regardless of this setting (only injection is gated) Disable if you notice prompt pollution or want to test agent behavior without historical bias Similarity Matching The service uses TaskIntelligenceService embeddings to find relevant historical learnings: Minimum similarity threshold: 0.4 (40%) Minimum quality threshold: 30 (out of 100) Maximum results: 3 learnings per prompt Project-scoped: Only learnings from the same project are considered Formatted Learning Context Learnings are injected into task descriptions as markdown: ## Historical Learnings from Similar Tasks ### Learning 1: <Task Title> (Similarity: 85%) **Outcome**: Success **Agent Configuration**: backend-developer, database-designer **Commands Used**: /build-feature **Execution Mode**: sequential **Duration**: 12.5 minutes **Errors Encountered**: - `ECONNREFUSED: Connection refused` → Resolved by starting PostgreSQL service - `Module not found: bcrypt` → Resolved by running npm install bcrypt **Key Decisions**: - Used JWT tokens instead of session cookies for better scalability - Implemented rate limiting at middleware level --- (Additional learnings follow same format) Configuration Constants Constant Value Purpose MAX_RESULTS 3 Maximum learnings injected per prompt MAX_OUTPUT_SIZE 10KB Maximum stored terminal output QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS 500 Timeout for similarity query (non-blocking) MAX_CONTEXT_SIZE 15KB Maximum formatted markdown context MIN_SIMILARITY 0.4 Minimum similarity threshold MIN_QUALITY 30 Minimum quality score threshold Fire-and-Forget Extraction Learning extraction is non-blocking to avoid slowing down task completion: Runs in background with Promise.catch() only Task update succeeds even if extraction fails Errors are logged but don't interrupt the workflow Timeout-Protected Injection Learning injection never delays task execution: Uses Promise.race with 500ms timeout If similarity query takes too long, task proceeds without historical context Prevents blocking the critical path for task execution Use Cases Error Prevention: Avoid repeating resolved errors from past tasks Best Practices: Propagate successful patterns and agent configurations Decision Guidance: Surface key decisions that led to good outcomes Efficiency: Reduce trial-and-error by learning from historical data Privacy & Scoping Learnings are project-scoped (no cross-project contamination) Terminal output is truncated to prevent sensitive data leakage Stored in local SQLite database (not shared externally) Disable feature entirely via settings if needed Agent Intelligence and your data (ADR-0026) Agent Memory and Cross-Task Learning are pinned to local AI processing. Extraction and similarity matching for both features run entirely on your local Ollama model — task content, terminal output, and stored memory or learning entries are never sent to a cloud AI provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or xAI), regardless of which provider you have selected elsewhere in CrewDeck. This is enforced in code, not just by convention: a privacy-pinned prompt that resolves to any non-Ollama provider is refused and routed to the local model instead. If Ollama is unavailable, extraction is skipped rather than retried remotely. Importing Shared Data New releases and summaries are imported into your local database Imported items are tagged with "Shared by @username" Import Behavior Idempotent: Importing multiple times is safe; duplicates are ignored Race-safe: Uses database unique constraints to prevent conflicts Filtered: Your own exports are automatically excluded during import Validated: Zod schema validation ensures data integrity Size-limited: Files larger than 1MB are rejected for safety Viewing Shared Data Imported releases appear in your Release Management view with: "Shared by @username" badge Full task list and metadata Read-only (cannot modify imported releases) Use Cases Team visibility: See what teammates have released Activity awareness: View daily summaries from other team members Coordination: Understand team progress without manual status updates Audit trail: Git history provides a complete record of shared data changes Configuration Settings → Team Data: Auto-export: Toggle automatic export on release/summary creation Sync status: View last export and import timestamps Manual controls: Export and import buttons for on-demand operations

CrewDeck implements an event sourcing pattern to maintain a complete, immutable audit trail of all state changes in the system. What is Event Sourcing? Event sourcing captures every state change as an append-only event in the state_events table. Instead of just storing current state, the system records every transition, allowing you to: Replay history to reconstruct past states Audit all changes for compliance and debugging Analyze patterns in how tasks and agents evolve over time What Events Are Captured The system tracks events for: Tasks: Created, updated status, assigned agents, dependencies added Agents: Discovered, updated, removed Releases: Created, updated, published Terminals: Session started, output written, session ended All other entities: Any state mutation triggers an event Event Structure Each event includes: Entity type: What was changed (task, agent, release, etc.) Entity ID: Which specific instance was changed Action: What happened (created, updated, deleted, etc.) Previous state: Snapshot of data before the change New state: Snapshot of data after the change Metadata: Additional context (user ID, timestamp, etc.) Timestamp: When the event occurred Viewing Event History Access event history through the API: // Get all events for a specific task const events = await window.api.events.getByEntity('task', taskId) // Filter events by action type const events = await window.api.events.list({ action: 'task:updated' }) // Count events in a time range const count = await window.api.events.count({ startDate, endDate }) Event Retention Events are retained for 90 days by default Cleanup runs automatically to remove expired events Maximum 1 million events stored at any time Old events are deleted in batches to avoid blocking Performance Optimizations Deferred writes: Events are batched using setImmediate() to avoid blocking the event loop Single transactions: Batched events are written in one transaction for efficiency Emergency flush: If more than 10,000 events are pending, emergency batch writes are triggered Sensitive data filtering: Fields like passwords and API keys are automatically stripped from snapshots Use Cases Debugging: Replay events to understand how a task reached its current state Compliance: Maintain audit trails for regulated environments Analytics: Analyze patterns in task state transitions Conflict resolution: Understand conflicting changes in collaborative scenarios Time travel: Reconstruct system state at any point in the past Architecture The event sourcing system uses a Change Data Capture pattern: Entity tables (tasks, agents) remain the source of truth State changes are written to entity tables as normal Events are recorded in parallel to state_events as an audit log Events never modify entities; they are append-only records

Demo Mode is a guided product tour: a scripted, zero-latency walkthrough of task execution, Debate and Duel that plays through CrewDeck's real screens using sample data. It is the fastest way to see what a finished run looks like — useful for evaluating CrewDeck, onboarding a teammate, or showing a colleague what the app does before connecting a single repository. Nothing a demo shows is real, and nothing it shows is saved. A demo makes no AI model call, runs no git command, opens no terminal session, talks to no GitHub, and writes nothing to your database. No project, task, agent, branch or pull request is created or modified. Whatever real work is running in the background keeps running, untouched. Turning Demo Mode On​ Demo Mode is off by default. To turn it on: Navigate to Settings > Sandbox & Terminal Find the Demo Mode section Toggle Demo Mode on Turning it on reveals the demo entry points described below. Turning it off hides them again; it never affects work already running. Starting a Tour​ There are two ways in: Entry point Where What it does Run Demo (in a project) Project header, under Resources Plays the tour without leaving the project. Exiting returns you to the Board. Run Demo (global) Bottom of the app sidebar Asks "Choose a project for the demo", then plays the tour. If you have no projects yet, it offers to create one first. Both entry points play exactly the same tour. What the Tour Covers​ The tour tells one continuous story: a fictional company, Northwind Freight, fixing duplicate freight bookings in a repository called northwind-freight/dispatch-api. It plays three segments in order: # Segment What you see 1 From task to pull request The golden path. A task is filed on the board, an agent claims it, an isolated worktree is reserved, the live activity and assistant panels stream the agent's reasoning and tool use, tests go green, the card reaches Done, and a pull request is waiting. 2 Agents argue it out A multi-agent debate. Three agents — backend-developer, database-designer and quality-reviewer — argue the approach through all five real debate phases: preparing a shared worktree, debating, committing the decision, pushing the branch, and opening a pull request. 3 Two arms, one winner A duel. Two agents attempt the same change two different ways — different models, different approaches, same starting commit — side by side and at the same time, each arm showing its own configuration and progress. At the end a decision panel promotes one arm and explains why. Every step is captioned. A caption bar inside each segment names what is happening and why, along with a Step N of M counter for the segment you are watching. Playback Controls​ A control bar sits at the bottom of the tour: Control Effect Pause / Resume Stops and restarts playback. Your position is kept exactly where it was. Skip segment Jumps to the start of the next segment. The segment you skipped still shows as finished. Segment buttons The row of segment titles above the controls. Click any one to jump straight to it — forwards or backwards. Restart Returns to the very beginning. Available at any time, including after the tour has ended. Jumping and restarting are instant: the tour is rebuilt from its script rather than replayed, so it can never land halfway through a step. A DEMO banner stays on screen the whole time, reading "Sample data — nothing here is real", along with the title of the segment currently playing. Press Esc at any point to leave the tour. Previewing a Single Feature​ With Demo Mode on, a small Preview button also appears next to the Create Task, Create Debate and Create Duel forms. It plays just the one segment relevant to that form, as a modal on top of the page you are on. Previews are designed to be interrupted: closing one returns you to exactly the form you left, with everything you had already typed still there. Nothing you were part-way through is lost. Ending the Tour​ When the last segment finishes, a completion screen appears with three choices: Button What it does Create a real project Closes the demo and opens the real project-creation form, so you can go straight from watching to doing. Cancelling that form leaves the demo behind and returns you to the app. Watch it again Replays the tour from the first step. Exit demo Leaves the tour and returns you to the app.

Monitor AI agent decision-making and execution phases in real-time. Viewing Agent Traces Open a completed task Navigate to the Traces tab (if agent emitted trace markers) View the agent's execution timeline with: Analysis phase (decisions, code structure analysis) Planning phase (reasoning, approach selection) Execution phase (tool usage, file operations) Verification phase (test results, validation) Trace Information Each trace entry shows: Phase badge (color-coded: Analysis=Blue, Planning=Purple, Execution=Green, Verification=Orange) Event type (decision, tool use, reasoning, output, error) Timestamp Event description Confidence score (0-100%) Expandable metadata with additional details Filtering Traces Use the filter bar to narrow down traces: Filter by phase (Analysis, Planning, Execution, Verification) Filter by event type (Decision, Tool Use, Reasoning, Output, Error) Search by description or agent name Phase Summary A footer displays the distribution of events across phases, helping you understand where the agent spent most of its time.

Get AI-powered agent suggestions based on task context and historical performance. Where Recommendations Appear When creating a new task In the agent selection dropdown Recommendations are marked with a star icon How Recommendations Work The system analyzes: Task title and description Historical agent success rates by task category Semantic matching between task content and agent capabilities Agent performance tracking data Recommendation Details Hover over a recommended agent to see: Match score (0-100%) Reason for recommendation Historical success rate for similar tasks

Run structured debates between AI agents to explore different perspectives on technical decisions. Creating a Debate Navigate to your project Click New Debate (next to New Task button) Enter a debate title (e.g., "Architecture Decision: Microservices vs Monolith") Provide a topic description with context Select 2 or more agents to participate from your project's agents Click Start Debate Debate Execution The debate wizard shows: Preparing: Creating debate context Debating: Agents discuss the topic (AI moderator facilitates) Committing: Saving debate transcript Pushing: Pushing to remote repository Terminal output streams in real-time showing the debate conversation. New in v0.11.0: Timer Display: A live timer shows elapsed time during the debate Background Mode: You can minimize the debate wizard and continue working on other tasks while the debate runs in the background Extended Timeout: Debates now have a 20-minute timeout (increased from 5 minutes) to support more thorough discussions Animated Output Panel: The terminal output panel has improved animations for better visual feedback Debate Output After completion: Debate transcript is saved to docs/debate/ in your repository File includes structured sections: Opening statements from each agent Discussion rounds (2-3) Synthesis of key points Conclusion and recommendations The transcript is committed and pushed to GitHub A searchable decision record is created in the Decision Journal You can review the markdown file to inform your decision Use Cases Architectural decisions Technology selection Approach comparison Problem analysis from multiple perspectives

The Decision Journal provides a searchable, filterable record of all decisions made through multi-agent debates. This feature helps teams track technical decisions, understand their rationale, and maintain institutional knowledge. Accessing the Decision Journal Navigate to any project Click the Decision Journal button (next to the New Debate button) The journal opens showing all debate decisions for the current project Full-Text Search Use the search bar at the top of the Decision Journal to search across: Decision titles Topics and descriptions Agent names Debate transcripts Tags Search is instant and highlights matching results. Filtering Decisions Filter decisions by: Status: All, Active, Implemented, Superseded, Rejected Tags: Any tags assigned to decisions (e.g., "architecture", "api-design", "performance") Filters can be combined with search to narrow results. Decision Details Each decision record shows: Title: The debate topic Status: Current decision status Date: When the debate occurred Participants: Which agents participated Tags: Categorization tags Summary: Key points and recommendations Full Transcript: Complete debate conversation (expandable) Exporting Decisions Click the Export button to download the decision journal: JSON format: Machine-readable with full metadata YAML format: Human-readable for documentation Exports include all decisions matching current search/filter criteria. Use Cases Review past architectural decisions and their rationale Onboard new team members with decision history Track decision implementation status Generate decision documentation for stakeholders Search for similar past decisions before making new ones

CrewDeck supports exporting and importing project configurations, enabling backup, migration, and sharing of project setups. Exporting Project Data Navigate to the project you want to export Click the Actions dropdown menu in the project header Select Export Project Choose format: JSON: Machine-readable, compact YAML: Human-readable, suitable for version control File is downloaded with naming convention: crewdeck-export-{project-slug}-{timestamp}.{format} What Gets Exported The export includes: Project metadata (name, description, slug) All repositories (GitHub connections, primary/context status) All agents (configurations, system prompts, personalities) All commands (scripts, descriptions, parameters) Task templates Configuration files Exports do NOT include: Task history and outcomes Git worktrees Authentication tokens Personal API keys Importing Project Data Navigate to the Projects page Click the Actions dropdown in the page header Select Import Project Choose a JSON or YAML export file Review the import preview showing what will be created Click Import to create the project Import Behavior Creates a new project (does not overwrite existing ones) If a project with the same slug exists, imports with a new slug GitHub repositories are created as disconnected (you must reconnect) Agents and commands are imported with all configurations You can safely import the same file multiple times Use Cases Backup: Export projects before major changes Migration: Move projects between CrewDeck installations Templates: Share project configurations with team members Version Control: Store YAML exports in Git for change tracking Testing: Create test environments from production exports
The Dashboard page provides application-wide analytics and a recent activity feed, giving visibility into task outcomes across all projects.

Navigate to the Dashboard (home icon in the sidebar) to see aggregated metrics at the top of the page. Metric Cards Metric Description Success Rate Percentage of tasks completed successfully across all projects Avg Duration Average time to complete tasks Avg Rating Average user satisfaction rating (1-5 stars) from task feedback PR Merge Rate Percentage of task Pull Requests that were merged on GitHub Status Breakdown Bar Below the date selector, a visual bar shows the distribution of task outcomes: Green segments for successful tasks Yellow segments for partial completions Red segments for failed tasks Gray segments for cancelled tasks Each segment displays the count and is labeled for accessibility. Date Range Filtering Use the date range selector to filter analytics by time period: Option Description 7d Last 7 days (default) 30d Last 30 days 90d Last 90 days All time All recorded outcomes

Below the analytics overview, the activity feed shows the 5 most recent task completions across all projects. The Daily Activity Summary widget on the Dashboard automatically generates a natural language summary of the past 24 hours of task activity across your projects. CrewDeck calculates a composite ranking score (0-100) for each agent based on historical task performance. Rankings help identify the best agents for specific tasks and inform the agent recommendation system.

The composite score is calculated from four weighted factors: Factor Weight Description Success Rate 40% Task completion rate, with partial success counting as half Efficiency 20% Execution time relative to category averages (faster = higher score) Satisfaction 25% User ratings mapped to a 0-100 scale Recency 15% Exponential decay with a 30-day half-life; rewards recently active agents

Rankings include a confidence indicator based on sample size: Sample Count Confidence Visual 10+ tasks Full (100%) Solid badge border 5-9 tasks Medium (50-99%) Standard badge 1-4 tasks Low (<50%) Dashed badge border Low confidence rankings are visually distinguished so you know to treat them cautiously.

Navigate to the Agent Performance page in the sidebar Scroll to the Outcome-Driven Rankings section The ranking leaderboard displays all agents sorted by composite score Top 3 agents are highlighted with a gold accent Leaderboard Columns Column Description Rank Position based on composite score Agent Agent name Score Composite score (0-100) Success Success rate component score Efficiency Efficiency component score Satisfaction Satisfaction component score Confidence Confidence percentage based on sample count Click column headers to sort by different metrics. Click an agent row to filter performance data.

Ranking badges appear on agent cards and recommendations throughout CrewDeck: Score Range Badge Color 80-100 Green 60-79 Blue 40-59 Yellow Below 40 Gray Hover over a ranking badge to see the full score breakdown tooltip, showing each factor's contribution and the confidence level.

When creating a task, agent recommendations now include ranking badges: Enter a task title and description Recommendations appear with ranking badges showing composite scores Hover over the badge to see the breakdown Click a recommendation to assign the agent Rankings are automatically recalculated when task outcomes are recorded.

CrewDeck creates isolated git worktrees for each task execution. Over time, these worktree folders accumulate and consume disk space. CrewDeck automatically cleans up worktrees when you rate a completed task.

When a task reaches "Done" status, you are prompted to rate it (see Rating Tasks) After you submit a rating, CrewDeck automatically removes the associated worktree folder The cleanup is non-blocking -- your rating is saved immediately, and cleanup runs in the background If cleanup fails (e.g., the worktree was already removed), the failure is logged but does not affect your rating

The cleanup process follows a robust approach: Step Action 1. Find worktree Scans the worktrees directory for the task's manifest file 2. Git remove Attempts git worktree remove --force to properly unregister the worktree 3. Fallback If git remove fails, directly deletes the folder and runs git worktree prune to clean stale references
To verify worktree cleanup, you can check the worktrees directory: # List active git worktrees git worktree list # Check the worktrees folder ls ~/Library/Application\ Support/crewdeck/worktrees/
